title: Ready to be handed to somebody else
items: The server runs in a container on Linux, which is how most people who host things host them. The image carries ffmpeg and writes everything to one volume. Five modules it imports by name had never been copied into it, so the wiring drawing, the traffic page, the theme and the update check all failed there; the image is now built and run and asked for every page before it is published, on both a desktop processor and ARM.
/health answers whether the server is up and nothing else - no name, no library, no addresses. It is what a container, a proxy or a monitor should ask, and it needs no invitation.

Nothing in what ships names a machine any more. An address of the house had been left as an example in three places, one of them beside an invitation token, and the server found its own address by probing one of them. It asks the routing table instead.
Nor does anything name a film. Comments explaining a fault by naming the release it happened to are the same fault as printing a library: the explanations are as clear without them.
The front page is a page rather than a mark on a wall: what it does, what it is not, both downloads, and an address to write to.

title: A server can report a fault, if it is told to
items: A setting under This server's code with three positions and no others: send nothing, send faults, or send faults with a description of this computer. It starts at nothing, and nothing is what it does until somebody changes it.

What never travels, whichever position it is in: the name of a film, a series or an episode; the name or address of anybody watching; an invitation key; a file path; the address of this machine or any other. Those are taken out on the way out rather than trusted not to appear - a stack trace is written by a program in a hurry and it puts whatever it has to hand into the message. The house's own names are taken out by name, because a person cannot be recognised by the shape of their name.

What the third position adds is a description of a computer and not of a person: how many cores, how much memory, which Windows, what the graphics card calls itself. That is the difference between "playback stopped" and "playback stopped on the machines with that card".

And any single fault can be sent by hand from Reports, whatever the setting says - with a question first that spells out what goes. Reading a fault, deciding it is worth passing on and pressing send is a different act from a machine reporting on itself.

title: A title that is not there is not a crash
items: Opening a series could take the app down. Every library numbers its own titles, so a season key belonging to the machine that keeps copies means nothing to the house server - and that plain not-found arrived as an exception nobody caught. A title that cannot be found is an empty screen now, and the log names the key and the machine that was asked, so the mix-up behind it can be seen rather than inferred from a stack trace.

title: Nothing moves between tabs
items: Settings used to be dropped from the bar on Films and TV to make room for the sort control, so a button moved and then vanished depending on which shelf was open. That is worse than a crowded row: the row scrolls, and a button off to the right is still where it was last time. Every control stays on every tab.

And the row of skins is headed Theme, with a line saying what it is: what your screens are drawn with, following you from server to server, overruled by a machine only while that machine has a reason to.

title: Update with it, actually
items: A machine set to take its builds from the one it follows never took any. It asks that machine what it is running and compares - and the answer was read out of the changelog file sitting beside the program, which the installer rewrites and which is missing altogether on a server run from source. So the number came back empty, the comparison had nothing to compare, and the switch did nothing while reading On.
A server now answers with the build it is actually running, which is the one place that cannot be wrong.

title: The pair, drawn from either side
items: The drawing made on the machine that keeps copies showed a box reading night server, none, not answering - a follower it does not have and never will. The other half of the pair, seen from there, is the house: it shows the machine it follows, by name and address.
And the dashes between the two run the way the film travels - out of the house and into the copy - whichever of the two the drawing was made on.

title: Update with what
items: The switch that makes a machine take its builds from the one it follows now names that machine. It read "update with it" back when the card could only be seen on the computer doing the following; read from the other side, on the machine it belongs to, it did not say with what.

title: Settings really do follow the server you picked
items: Picking a machine and opening Settings still showed this computer's name and this computer's settings. The page is a second script, and which server was chosen lived in the first one's own scope - readable from the second only by grace and ordering. A page that quietly reads nothing looks exactly like a page that read the wrong thing, which is what this was.
The chosen machine is stated plainly now rather than inferred across scripts, so the heading names it and every setting on the page belongs to it.

title: Every machine filed where it answers
items: Only the server being watched was ever checked against its own addresses, so a phone could sit in front of a list saying a machine was on this network while nothing from it would load. Every machine in the list is now filed under whichever of its addresses answers from where the screen is - the short way when that works, the other when the filed one does not.

And the list is read when it opens rather than once for the life of the screen. A machine re-filed after that list was drawn showed under one heading in the picker while the settings page, which reads it fresh, said the other thing.

title: Boxes that fit, arrows that point the right way
items: Every box in the drawing is as wide as the longest thing written in it. An address is as long as it is, and a box sized by guesswork either clipped it or left a gap.
A machine standing by is drawn dim rather than red. Red is for something that ought to answer and does not, and using it for both is why half the drawing looked like a fault.
The dashes between this machine and the router run the way the film travels - out of the server, through the router - rather than into it.

And the settings page takes the name from the machine whose settings are on the screen. It was working the name out from the row it had been picked from, which named this computer while another one's settings were shown.

title: Two sources means two machines
items: A film said it was coming from two sources while the second machine did not hold it at all. Splitting a film needs two things and only one was checked: the same file name, which is what says the bytes are identical, and a different machine, which is the entire point. Without the second, a film could be split between two addresses of one computer - one computer doing twice the work and reporting it as a share.
Both are checked now, and when a split is refused the log says which half failed and between which addresses.

title: Up goes back to the tabs
items: Pressing up from Casual play landed on the server name. That name became a button when it was made pressable, and it sits above the tabs - so the nearest thing above the content stopped being the row of tabs and became that, which is a long way from where anybody pressing up is trying to go.

title: Standby
items: The machine that keeps copies is tagged standby in the server list and beside the name at the top, in both the app and the web. It is what the machine is for - the one that answers when the other does not - rather than a description of what is on its disk.
And the tag disappears on the machine being used, because a machine you are watching is not standing by for anything.

title: What may move by day, and who may change it
items: Watchlists may fill while people are up, or wait for the night with everything else - a setting, since a house on a thin line would rather nothing moved at all in the evening. What somebody starts watching this minute waits for the night either way: by then this machine is the one that will be awake, and by day the house is answering for itself.

And the machine that keeps copies can be told to accept its settings from the server it follows, so nobody has to walk to a computer in a cupboard to change a number. Off unless somebody turns it on there; only that server, and only by its address.

title: Chasing the screen is a night job
items: What somebody started watching this minute is fetched at night, not by day. At night this machine is the one that will be awake, so the episode after the one on screen has to be here before the house sleeps; by day the house is answering for itself, and chasing every episode somebody starts spends the link on a copy nobody needs for hours. Watchlists and what people are part-way through go on quietly either way.
The word here is gone from the server list - the address in use already says which one it is.

title: Lines that start where the boxes end
items: A box works out its own height from what is written in it, and the lines into it were drawn from a height worked out separately - which is how a line came to start inside one box and stop short of the next. Both use the same number now.
The router reaches the machine that keeps copies along its short side, the edge facing the router, rather than dropping onto the top of it.

title: A pass is forty films, not forty subtitles
items: A five-gigabyte film sat at the top of the queue for a day while the queue said it was next and nothing went wrong with it. A pass fetches forty files and stops; the list held fifty subtitles ahead of that film, each a few kilobytes, each spending one of the forty. The pass ran out of allowance before it ever reached the film - every pass, all day.
Subtitles ride along with their film now and do not count against what a pass is worth.
The settings page says which machine's settings are on the screen, beside the word Settings.

title: One set of figures, not two
items: The Data sent box is gone. It counted the same two things the Watched and Copied rows already count, in a second shape, on the same page - and two tables of one truth is one table too many.

title: Whose setting is it
items: Two kinds of setting, and only one of them belongs to a machine. What a person keeps - how their subtitles look, what language they want, the skin, their quality ceilings - is theirs on every screen and every server they open, and changing servers does not change any of it.

What a machine keeps - its folders, its port, what it follows, when it sleeps - belongs to that machine. Those now go to whichever server is open in the bar, with that server's key, so picking one and being shown this one's port is over. Only the owner of a machine may change its settings, which the machine decides for itself rather than taking anybody's word.

The drawing names the machine and shows the address it answers to. The row of screens says who they are - by name where the server knows one, by address otherwise - and the machine that keeps copies is no longer listed among them, since it has a box of its own.

title: How much to keep, and what goes first
items: Two settings under Follow another server. A programme somebody put on a watchlist can be kept as far as the night needs, or every unwatched episode of it - which is what somebody usually means by putting a whole series on a list.

And what goes when there is no room left under the cap: the file nobody has touched for longest, which is the one nobody will miss, or the largest, which frees the most room in a single deletion and is what is wanted when one film is standing in the way of ten episodes. Nothing on the list is ever deleted either way.
The hours setting is called what it is - hours to sync to cache - rather than describing when the machine happens to be awake.

title: Which way in, chosen or worked out
items: The server chip at the top says lan or wan for the address in use, and the other one is a press away. The app picks whichever answers and mostly that is right, but when it is not, the person looking at the screen knows which network they are on and the machine does not.

Whether a person is handed the address this server answers to on its own network is now a setting beside what the copy keeps for them. They always have the way in from outside, which is the one that works from where they are; the other is an address inside somebody's house, and handing it to everyone who ever got a link should be a decision rather than an accident.
And the servers on each side of the router are listed by name.

title: A machine has a name
items: The app showed the house server as four numbers because the name was only ever put together where the web client asks for it - everything else looked in the settings file, found nothing there, and printed an address at somebody. The name travels with the addresses now, and a row filed under an address takes the name the machine gives.
And it can be chosen: a box on This server's code, with the computer's own name standing in it as the default. Empty means the computer's name, which is what it was before anybody thought to ask.

title: Any one address gets all four
items: Adding either machine now finds the other, and both of each one's addresses come with it. The house has always named its own two and the copy's two; the copy now names its own two and repeats the house's, which it asks for while the house can still be asked - because the hour it holds them for is the hour it cannot.
So somebody handed any single address ends up with all four, and every screen has a way in from either side of the router to either machine.

title: Both addresses, on the row and in hand
items: Every server row shows both of its addresses, each labelled lan or wan, with a note on the one in use. Which address a machine is filed under is the thing that goes wrong, and it cannot be checked when only one of them is on the screen.

On mobile data the app had nothing to fall back to but the copy. The other address of a machine was learned by asking that machine - and the case it exists for is precisely the one where the machine cannot be reached. It is taken from the row now, before anything is asked, so a phone opening a row filed under a house address goes straight out to the front door.

title: The short way round is preferred
items: A phone that had once learned a machine from away kept reaching it the long way round for good - out to the router and back in to a computer three metres away. That works, which is exactly the trouble: the address answered, so nothing ever went looking for the short one. When a machine has an address on this network and it answers, that is the one used.

And the name on a row follows the address it opens. A row calling itself by one address while reaching the machine at another is how an evening gets spent looking at the wrong thing - which is how this was found.

title: Nothing on the list is swept away
items: What the machine that keeps copies protects from deletion is now the whole list, not the part of it a pass happened to reach. A pass stops after forty files, and everything past that point was unprotected and swept away at the end of it to stay under the cap - which is where a watchlist went: named as wanted, never reached, deleted the same night, asked for again the next.

How far ahead to keep is now the length of the night rather than a number beside it. Four hours of episodes is no use across a ten-hour night, and somebody starting a series at midnight should not run out at four. The number in the settings is a floor; what decides it is how long this machine is the only one awake. From the last episode each person watched, forward, for every person the copy is kept for.

title: Told when the copy is made under you
items: Whoever is watching a film is told when the night server starts taking a copy of that same film, and told again when it lands - from that moment the evening survives the house server going off, which is the only reason anybody cares.
Only a copy made while somebody is watching is said out loud. One that was already there before the film started is not news, and a notice for it would be a notice at the start of every film.

title: The door that answers is the one that opens
items: A phone on the house network could sit in front of an empty library while the streamer beside it was fine. The difference was which address each had the machines filed under: the address a server is filed under is the one it happened to be learned by, and that says nothing about where the screen is standing now. A copy learned from a train is filed under the way in from outside, and back at home that address goes out to the router and back - when it works at all.

So a machine is now re-filed under whichever of its two addresses suits where the screen is, and when the app opens a server whose address does not answer it opens it by the one that does. Both addresses stay on the row either way round.

The servers page in both the app and the web is split under two headings - on this network, and from outside - because the two kinds of address behave differently and which one a machine is filed under is exactly the thing that goes wrong. Seeing it grouped is how you tell in one glance.

title: What would not come, and why
items: A file that sits at the top of the queue and never moves now says what happened to it. The machine that keeps copies held one error string and the next success wrote over it, so something failing every pass all night left no trace by morning and the only way to ask was to watch it live. It keeps the last dozen instead - the file, what went wrong, when, and how many times - and they are listed under the queue.
A row that will not move is either a file that keeps failing or a disk with no room left under its cap, and from the outside those look identical.

title: It can always find its way home
items: A phone on the house network could stop loading anything while the same servers answered a browser beside it. Falling back to a server's own outside address is not standing by - it is the same library the long way round - and the flag that says so was also the one the way home was checked against. So a screen that fell out through the router during a restart stayed out through it, and on the house network that route is the slow one at best.

The way home is tried whenever there is one, once a minute, with the request that was going to be made anyway. The address it was using becomes the other way in, so the next fall is as quick as this one was.

title: Told both addresses while it can still ask
items: The app showed only the address a server was typed in under, which away from home is the one that cannot be reached. It now writes both on the row - the one on that network and the one the router forwards - with a lan or wan tag on each.

Learned while at home, because that is when it can be: a screen on a train cannot ask a machine it cannot reach where else that machine lives. The server hands over both of its own addresses in the same answer that names the machine keeping copies, which every screen asks for the moment it opens.

title: The house has a front door too
items: Away from home the app showed a light beside both servers and drew nothing at all - no shelves, no posters. A light is a knock on whichever address answers, and the library was still being asked of the one that does not: a server learned at home is filed under its address on that network, and from a train that address answers nothing.

Every screen already knew to fall back to the machine that keeps copies. None of them knew to try the house's own front door, which is the same library with all of it on rather than a fraction. A server now says where else it can be reached, and that address is tried first - the copy after it.

title: One row per machine, and the right name for the engine
items: Adding a server matches the machine rather than the address it was typed as, so the same one learned by its other way in no longer arrives as a second row. Rows that turn out to be one machine are folded together and written down that way when the app starts - deliberately, on the stored list, which is not the same as saving what a screen happens to be showing.

A film playing from a machine with no card and no encoder is no longer labelled a transcode on somebody else's graphics chip. Every machine says what it encodes with now, and one that cannot encode at all says so: what arrives from it is the file as it stands, and the line along the top of the picture says exactly that.

title: A tab for the other machine
items: Settings has a Remote computer tab. Everything about a computer that is not this one lives there - the server this machine follows, what it is asked to keep, and the keys it needs to fetch subtitles and look titles up for itself. They had been mixed in with this machine's own switches, where two kinds of thing read as one long list.

The copying is counted the way the watching is: this week, this month, altogether - gigabytes, files, titles, the largest one and where it went - in a row of its own under the viewing figures. Watching and copying are the two things this server does with a disk and a network, and a heavy week of one with a quiet week of the other is a different machine from the reverse.

The panels in the drawing are as tall as the words in them. The first line sits a set distance below the top of a box and each one after it lower again, so a two-line panel drawn at the height of a one-line panel wrote its second line underneath itself.

And a transfer that brings down nothing at all - the other machine restarting, or a connection that went before the first block - says so, rather than reporting that what arrived is not a film. It was not a bad file; there was no file.

Asking the machine that keeps copies to write a subtitle now asks the machine that can. That one has no speech model - it is three gigabytes and there is no card there to run it on - and it used to answer that it could not and stop. The film is named by what it is rather than by a number, since the other machine files it under its own; the subtitle it writes lands beside its copy and travels here on the next pass like any other file beside a video.

And a queue that has stopped moving because the cache is full to its cap says so, with what it holds, what it is allowed and what is free on the disk. Full is not broken, and from the outside the two look the same.

title: A machine is up if any of its doors opens
items: The machine that keeps copies showed red in the server list while it was sitting there working. It was knocked on at one address and called down when that one did not answer - and the address it is filed under from outside does not answer from inside the house, which says nothing about the machine. Every door it has is tried now, and the server's own word counts too: it hears from that machine every few seconds, which a browser on the far side of a router cannot always do.

The queue has moved off This computer and onto Now playing, where the people watching are: what is being fetched and who is watching are two halves of what this server is doing this minute. What it has already transferred stays where it was.

And a subtitle no longer takes a place in the queue. It is a few kilobytes travelling with its film, and three of them under one title made a numbered list read like a mess; the count is noted instead.

Who is following this server, and everything that has gone to them, have moved to Now playing as well. They are what this server is doing rather than how it is set up, and This computer is for the setting-up.

And the words in the drawing stay inside their panels. An address long enough to leave its box used to write itself across whatever was beside it; the full text is still there when the pointer rests on it.

The machine that keeps copies says how full it is when it announces itself - what it holds, how much it is allowed, and what is left on the disk - and that is on its row under Now playing. It is the only machine that can measure its own disk, and "is there room for tonight" is what anybody looking at that row is asking.

Forty files fetched a pass, not forty looked at. The list carries everything worth having and most of it is already on that disk; counting those against the window meant a machine holding a hundred and twenty files never reached the films at the bottom of the list, and the queue read as a row of things that were never taken.

title: One order, kept from end to end
items: The queue is a numbered list and it is worked through from the top. The machine with the library on it decides the order - whoever is watching, then anything moved up by hand, then the rest - and the machine that keeps copies now takes it exactly as given. It had been sorting the list again on arrival and putting hand-moved files back on top, so a film somebody had moved up hours earlier was fetched while the person on the sofa waited for their next episode. The list arrived right and was spoiled on arrival.
An episode already mentioned by some other shelf keeps the better claim: three episodes of what somebody was watching sat below a film nobody had started, because a watchlist had named them first.
The queue shows its numbers, and says why each row is where it is - watching now, or moved up.
And it appears on Now playing under its own heading, which is the other half of what this server is doing right now.

title: Whoever is watching leads the queue
items: What somebody is watching this minute, and the episodes after it, now come before everything else the machine that keeps copies is asked to take - including a film moved to the front by hand. Pinning used to beat everything, so a seventeen-gigabyte film asked for hours ago was fetched at full speed while the person on the sofa waited for the next episode of what they were in the middle of. Three ranks now: whoever is watching, then what was asked for, then the rest.
The count of episodes fetched ahead is the one already set - what is on screen, then forward through that series until either the hours or the episode count runs out.

title: Nothing is held back, only ordered
items: Big files used to wait for a quiet house. In a house where somebody is nearly always watching that meant they were never fetched at all - a seventeen-gigabyte film sat at the head of the queue for an evening, and the one somebody had just started would have sat there for the next one. Everything on the list is taken now; the only question is what comes first, which is what a person moved to the front, then what arrives in a minute or two, then the rest.
And a big file being fetched is not interrupted when somebody starts watching, which was tried and was worse: the fetch would have stood aside every evening and finished on none of them.

And the catalogue key travels with the subtitle key: one button sends both to the machine that keeps copies, which is what puts posters on its shelves instead of a grid of grey rectangles when the house cannot be reached.

title: The queue reads in the order it will happen
items: What is still to come stands above what has already arrived. The order inside each half is the order the other machine will work in, and a list that reads top to bottom should not put a dozen finished rows between the thing being fetched and the thing after it. Anything moved to the front by hand stays at the front.

A big file being fetched now stands aside when somebody starts watching. Both machines share the same link, and seven gigabytes arriving at full speed is felt by whoever is in front of a screen. What has come down is kept, and the next pass carries on from that byte - so standing aside costs nothing but time. A file somebody moved to the front by hand is not interrupted: it was asked for.
The OpenSubtitles key is shown in Settings under Subtitles, in full, with a button to copy it and another to send it straight to the machine that keeps copies.

title: Saying which machine came back empty
items: A shelf that arrives empty now writes down which machine was asked and what it answered. Films and TV have come up blank on one screen while the server hands out a hundred and twenty films to the same key from the same network, and that is not a thing to keep guessing at from the outside.

title: Asking the machine the film is on
items: "Cannot read this title just now" when the subtitle or sound menu was opened on a film coming from the machine that keeps copies. The key in hand is that machine's number for the film and no other machine knows it, but the lookup went to whichever server the app was pointed at - so a film playing from the copy could not be described by the server it was not on. Seven lookups now ask the machine actually serving the film.

The subtitle and sound menus open whether or not the film can be looked up. The tracks inside the file are what those menus are mostly for and the player already knows them; the catalogue is only needed for what could be fetched, and a menu that refuses to open because a lookup failed is a menu that cannot be used at all.
The eyes are gone.
And the House look keeps whatever colour you draw with rather than replacing it with the machine's default.

The home screen stopped waiting on the machine that keeps copies. Everything on it came from the server it copies, so asking it for the same shelves added a round trip each to the slower of the two machines and put nothing new on screen. It is still in the list, still opened and switched to - it is simply not asked twice for the same film.
The subtitle key field was reading the viewer's settings, where it has never lived; it reads the library's own now, and the button that sends it to the copy had taken a name the server already used.

title: Skins, held by the server
items: The look is a skin now, and it can be changed: House, Night server, Arcade, Paper and Phosphor, chosen per person in Settings on the web and in the app. The palettes live on the server rather than being written into three clients in two languages, so adding one is an entry in a file and every screen wears it the next time it asks.

Two of them are nobody's choice. The machine that keeps copies wears its own after dark - a colder ground and a pair of eyes up in the banner, blinking a little out of step - and a machine whose card has been given to a game wears the loud one and sends the house to the copy while it lasts. Both overrule what was picked, say so, and hand it back when they pass.

The server list in the web opens above the shelves at last. The bar carries a backdrop filter, which makes it the containing block for anything fixed inside it as well as a stacking context of its own, so no z-index could ever have lifted it - the list is moved out of the bar when it opens and positioned under the name by hand.

Picking a server in the web now means something: the shelves come from the one that was picked rather than staying merged, which is why choosing the machine that keeps copies appeared to do nothing at all.

And the whole web client falls over to it. A page cannot fetch its way out of a server that is off, so the address is handed over while it still answers - the first request that fails for want of a server is retried there, and everything after it comes from there.
The drawing names both ways in from outside, one per machine, and the router box is wide enough for what is written in it.

The OpenSubtitles key sits where subtitles are set instead of being buried in Library, with a button that sends it to the machine that keeps copies - which fetches subtitles for what it takes, and without a key of its own was taking films half the house cannot read.
And the note about the server having changed version is said once per version rather than every time the app is opened. What it remembered lived in memory, so every return was a first look.

Forgetting one server no longer takes others with it. The list was folded whenever it was written, and the screens show a folded list - so anything that saved what it was showing threw away every row that had been folded into another. Folding is for drawing now; what is written down is written as given, and Forget removes every address of the one machine it stands for.

title: A queue that moves, and a list that shows everything
items: A file moved to the front of the queue by hand now goes whatever the hour. Big files are held back while anybody is watching, which is right for a list the machine works out and wrong for one a person put in order: a seventeen-gigabyte film sat at the head of the queue for a whole evening because somebody was watching television for a whole evening.

The machine that keeps copies says what build it is running when it announces itself, and the drawing on This computer shows it beside the name. Two machines on different builds speak slightly different languages to the same app.

The server list in the web offers the copy, which was missing from it - the server hands its address over, which is the whole point, and a list that leaves out the one machine still answering is the wrong list. It also has both of its addresses under it.
And the list draws above the shelves rather than behind them. The bar is a stacking context of its own, so no z-index inside it could ever lift the menu clear.

The copy stopped arriving as a new row every time. It was matched against the server it copies, and that server answers to two addresses as well, so reaching the house the other way learned the same machine again. Rows are folded whenever the list is written now, not only when it is shown.

title: Both doors, the right wiring, and Reports where it belongs
items: A machine answers to two addresses - the one on this network and the one the router forwards - and the web now knows both. Each server is asked which machine it is and how else it can be reached, so the picker shows one row per machine with both doors under it, each with its own light, and opening a machine takes whichever door answers from where the page is.

The drawing on This computer was wrong: everything hangs off the router, both machines and every screen, so it sits in the middle with room around it and the way in from outside comes down into it. The only line that is not the router's doing is the one between the two servers, which is one of them copying from the other.
The watch log has a filter for what the machine that keeps copies is holding - which is the question that page is opened with once the house server is off.
Reports is a page inside Settings rather than a tab on the bar, and its count has gone back on the gear. The bar is for places to look at films.

title: No window left behind
items: Taking an update from inside the app left a command window sitting in the temporary folder. The shell that does the work is started without a window, but the thing it starts makes a console of its own whatever it was told, and minimised is not hidden. It runs in place now, and closes itself when it is done.

title: The router, and one question instead of three
items: The drawing on This computer now shows the router the house goes out through, with its address, and pressing it opens the page it serves - which is where a port forward is set and where it is undone.

It asks the server one question rather than three, and every twelve seconds rather than five. On a machine at the end of a slow link that was three round trips for one picture, several times a minute.
The line along the top of a film now begins with the machine the bytes are coming from. After a film has moved house that is the only thing about the picture that has changed, and nothing said so.
And the web has the same server chip in the bar: it names the machine this page is reading, and pressing it lists the others with a light each, knocked on as the list opens.

One row per machine, not per address. A server learned at home and the same machine reached from away were both in the list, so the house appeared twice under two names and moving between them looked like moving between machines. They carry the same id and are folded on it now, with a lan or wan tag on the row saying which way in it is using.

title: Said once, and pressable with a thumb
items: The note about the night server holding a smaller selection is read once and stays away. It was remembered inside the screen rather than on the device, so every rotation and every return from a film brought it back.
The server name at the top is now a proper button rather than a line of small text: big enough for a thumb on a phone, and still a single press on a remote.

Switching servers keeps the address it actually opened. A machine reached by a different address from away was not in the list under that name, so "the current server" quietly resolved to the first one instead and drew its library under the other one's name.

title: Two moods a machine can be in
items: The machine that keeps copies now looks like itself after dark: a colder, darker palette across the app and the web, and a pair of eyes in the top of the banner that blink a little out of step with each other. It holds a fraction of the library and it is not the machine anybody chose, so it should be obvious at a glance which one is on screen.

Game mode gets the opposite treatment - bright, saturated, impossible to miss - and now sends the house to the copy while it lasts, because a card that has been handed to a game is not encoding anything.
Neither is a setting. Both are the machine saying what is already true about it, and the screens ask every ten minutes because the hour turns.
A subtitle is no longer blamed when a server goes off: the same fault reaches the player as an unreadable file, and it was dropping the subtitles and saying so at every handover.

title: Moving house, properly this time
items: A film that loses its server now carries on from the machine that keeps copies. Four things had to be right before it could: the player never knew what it was playing - the details were only fetched when somebody opened a panel - so every attempt looked up nothing and gave up; copied files arrived unmeasured, so the app asked for an encode the spare machine cannot do; a server that has been switched off drops packets rather than refusing them, so each attempt hung for twenty seconds; and there was nothing in the log to say any of it. Tested by pulling the server out from under a running episode: it picked up one second after where it stopped, playing the file as it stands.
The whole app goes with the film, so leaving it lands on the copy menu and what plays next comes from there too.

The server name at the top of the app opens the list of servers - each knocked on as it opens, so an address that is off is not offered as though it were there - and pressing one moves to it and says where it went.

title: What is in a copied file, and where you are
items: Files taken by the machine that keeps copies arrived unmeasured - no codec, no size, no duration - because it never opens them. A player handed one of those will not risk sending it as it stands: it asked for an encode instead, of a file it could have played untouched, and a spare box with no card in it answered that with a fault and a stopped picture. The measurements now travel with the file, and everything already copied is filled in from the house.
And if an encode cannot start at all, the file is sent as it is rather than nothing.
The top of the app now says which server the shelf came off, with a dot beside it and a word when it is the copy.

title: Two seconds a page, gone
items: Every reply longer than about 1.4 kB was taking exactly 2.15 seconds to arrive over the network while the server itself had answered in 17 milliseconds: headers and body leave as two writes, and the second was waiting to be acknowledged before it went. Short replies fitted in one packet and were instant, which is what made it look like a slow machine instead of a stalled socket. Turned off, and a shelf listing arrives in a hundredth of a second.

title: A readout instead of three lists
items: This computer opens with a drawing of where everything goes: the way in from outside, this server, the screens that are on, and the machine that keeps copies. A box is lit when it is doing something and a line carries moving dashes while bytes are on it, so the three questions asked every evening - is the other machine up, is anybody watching, can the house be reached - are answered at a glance.
It redraws every five seconds and reads what it shows from what the server already knows; nothing extra is asked of anything.

title: A film off two machines at once
items: Where both servers hold the same file - and a copy is only kept when its fingerprint agrees with the original - the app now reads it off both at once, two megabytes at a time. Each machine takes the next lump it is free to take, so a link twice as quick carries twice as much without anything being measured.
Which makes losing one of them nothing to look at: the survivor picks up the lump the other had taken on and the picture does not stop. The line along the top says which share came from where.
Only a file being served as itself is split. A transcode is made as it is sent, so two of them are not the same bytes.

title: It moves before the picture stops
items: The app now finds the same film on the machine that keeps copies while everything is still fine, so a switch is a seek to the same second rather than a search made with the frame frozen.
And it goes when the buffer runs thin - six seconds under eight seconds in hand, or five seconds stopped - instead of waiting for the stream to fail and two retries to fail after it.

title: The near server's copy wins
items: Where two servers hold the same film, the card that survives is the one from whichever answered quickest when it was last asked - so a machine in the cupboard is what plays, not the same film from two hundred milliseconds away. Each knock is timed; nothing extra is asked.
And the shelves fill as the answers come: every server is asked at once rather than one after another, and one on a bad line no longer holds up the screen for the rest - it simply misses that draw.

title: Every file on the copy is a file the house knows about
items: The machine keeping copies held ninety-four files and told the house about twenty-six: it only knew the names of what had been on a list since it started keeping one, so everything copied before that - the films - sat there unmarked. It asks the master what the strangers are called, once, and writes the answers down.

title: Whose server it is, asked rather than assumed
items: A server added by invitation wore the guest badge for ever, even at home where that same machine calls you its owner. Whose it is comes from the server now, asked each time the list is drawn - it is the server that decides, by the address a request arrives on.

title: One row, two doors
items: Switching to the machine that keeps copies gave an empty library: it is added hidden, so its shelf does not stand beside the same films from the server it copies - and hidden had just been made to mean hidden even for the server you are on. Opening a server shows it.

That machine is one row with both of its addresses on it - the one on the network and the one from outside - and the key in use. Switching to it tries whichever answers from where you are standing, so a copy learned on the sofa still opens from a train.
Its light is lit if either address answers.

title: What is on the copy is on it for everybody
items: The machine keeping copies tells the house about everything on its disk, not only what is on today's list: a film copied last week for one person is still there, still plays for anyone, and now still wears its green dot. It remembers what each file is called on the machine it came from, beside the copies.
And it says so plainly when somebody lands on it - how many films and episodes it holds, all playable by anyone who may watch there, and separately what was kept for them.

title: A guest may ask where the copy is
items: Somebody watching from away was refused the question outright, so their page decided this server keeps no copy - and their posters wore no green dot either. An invitation may ask where the machine keeping copies is, and which titles it holds.

title: The copy shows up while you are looking at the list
items: Opening Servers asks whichever server is in use whether it keeps a copy somewhere, so that machine appears in the list there and then - with the key already in it - rather than only after the app is started again.

A guest watching from away has a Night server screen of their own: which machine keeps the copy, whether it is awake, and their own link to it, to keep - because once this server is off a page cannot go looking for one.

The library takes two at once. A machine keeping copies asks what is worth keeping every minute while somebody is watching and a scan is writing, and the old journal shuts every reader out for as long as a writer holds it: thirty faults in one evening, all of them "database is locked". It uses the write-ahead log now, and waits its turn where it must.

title: The copy finds its own files
items: Nothing on the machine keeping copies ever got a name or a poster: it looked the files up by their whole path, and the same file is written one way by whoever typed the folder with one kind of slash and another way by whoever typed the other. It matches by name now, and says so when it cannot.

title: A copy that looks like itself while it fills
items: What has arrived on the machine keeping copies is named and given its poster every few files, and again while a long pass runs - rather than only when the whole pass ends, which with a dozen big files is an hour of blank shelves.

title: The copy looks like a library, and says it is there
items: What the machine keeping copies holds arrives with its name and its pictures: it can reach the house over the network and the catalogue over the internet, and the second is not always there - which is what a shelf of grey rectangles was.
Servers in the app carry a light: green for a machine that answered a moment ago, red for one that did not. Every server in the list is asked, not only the one in use.
Forget asks first, and says what goes with it - an address can be typed again, a key handed out by somebody else cannot.
The machine that keeps copies can be put back in one press after being forgotten.
Hidden means hidden, even for the server that is open: its films stay off the shelves while it goes on answering about settings.
When this server stops answering, the browser offers the copy and opens it in a tab of its own - with the guest's own link, so nobody has to be told an address.
And the server says whether the copy is awake, so a client knows before it needs to.
The queue can be ordered by hand, with arrows, and says what has gone lately - the last ten transfers, what they were, how big, and which machine they went to. Check log shows the lot.

A server says which build it is running rather than reading it off a file beside itself: building an installer rewrote that file, and the machine then reported a version it was not running - which is how one a build behind called itself up to date.
A server is its own library, whatever a browser happens to have remembered. Opening the machine that keeps copies said it could not reach a server at undefined.

One tray and one server to a machine. An installer that starts the program while the shortcut is bringing it up left two of each - Windows lets the second bind a port the first already holds, so it answered nobody while scanning the same library.

title: The next episodes come with the one being watched
items: The episodes after what somebody is watching are second on the copy list rather than fortieth. They were worked out last, so by the time the other machine reached them the evening was over.
What the copy will take, in order, is a list on the page - with a button to take one next when the order is wrong.
One pass at a time: Sync now and the round that comes every minute both started one, and two of them copied the same film twice.
Sync now works from the page it is on rather than answering nothing.

title: What somebody is watching goes first
items: What is on a screen this minute leads the list of what the other machine should keep - and it never did: the question was asked of the panel's answer, which does not carry that list, so nothing playing ever reached the front of the queue.

While somebody is watching, the copy takes only what arrives in a minute or two - their next episode, a subtitle - and leaves the seventeen-gigabyte film nobody has started until the house is quiet. It carries on from where it stopped.

Subtitles sitting beside a film travel with it: the languages the people it is kept for read, and whichever was chosen for that title. A film on the other machine with no subtitle is a film half the house cannot watch.
The green dot appears on shelves that were already drawn when the answer about the other machine arrives, rather than only on the next thing drawn.

Following can be stopped in the middle of a file. Turning it off left the transfer already in flight reading somebody's disk for another hour; it is put down between lumps now, and the next pass asks for the rest rather than the whole thing.

title: A season of ticks does not empty the shelf
items: Continue watching was built from the sixty newest notes about where somebody had got to. Marking a season watched writes one of those per episode, so a hundred and twenty ticks filled the lot and every half-watched film fell off the end - nine of them, down to one. It looks six hundred back now, which is only how far it looks, not how much it shows.

Check on either server row asks the site again rather than repeating what that machine last heard: a server keeps its answer for a while, so the other machine went on saying it was up to date and the Update button never appeared.

title: Ticks that survive a restart
items: Every tick anybody had made was wiped each time the server started. The place where a viewer's progress is kept was being rebuilt on every single start - the test for the old shape was true of the new one as well - and the rebuild carried only the columns it knew about, so the marks went with it. The table is left alone now, and a rebuild carries whatever it holds.
The ticks lost to that are recognised on the way back: a row at the very beginning of something nobody has ever played is a tick whose mark was thrown away.
And nothing sits on Continue watching at nought minutes: a row at the start of a film is not something to carry on with, which is why cards were wearing a progress bar at the very beginning.

title: The copy keeps its own name
items: A following server is a second machine, not a second person: the places that arrive under the house's own name are filed against whoever owns that machine, and go back under the house's name when they return. It no longer takes the name of the person it copies for.

It says what it holds before the copying starts as well as after it. A pass that fetches two seven-gigabyte films runs for an hour, and until it ended the house was told nothing - so nothing wore a green dot all day.
And it keeps talking during that hour: announcing itself, taking the places, saying what is here. The copying runs beside that rather than instead of it.
Sync now in Another server builds the list again and takes what is missing, instead of waiting for the minute to come round.

title: The end of a row is the end of the row
items: Walking right along a programme's seasons ran out of seasons and left the row - upwards, onto Mark all unwatched, where left and right did nothing and the remote was stuck. The row keeps the remote now; up and down are the way out of it.
An episode already watched is not copied to the machine that keeps them, and the run of episodes ahead steps over it: six ahead means six nobody has seen.

title: Replace the other machine from here
items: The app's Updates has a second row for the machine that keeps copies: what it is running, and a button that replaces it - without switching the whole app over to it and back again. It answers the same way the server does, and says what it is running when it returns.

A following server can be told to update with the one it follows: when the house is on a newer build it takes the same update it would have been given from its own settings page, from the same place and checked against the same hash. Off unless asked for.

title: Read once, and a dot per episode
items: The night server's line takes a press: Right puts it away, and it stays away for that machine.
Episodes wear the green dot as well as posters, so a season says how much of it is on the other machine before the evening it matters.
A following server adopts the folder its copies land in, and takes the house's catalogue key, so what it holds arrives as films with posters rather than as a list of file names on an empty shelf.

An episode ticked as watched stayed unwatched, and a series went on saying 11 of 12: the tick wrote a resume point at the end of the film, and the machine then argued with it because the log showed nobody had sat through that episode. A tick is now recorded as a tick, and settles it.
Marking something watched takes its resume point away rather than leaving it two seconds from the credits, and Continue watching hands over to the next episode.
The watch log showed the newest four hundred viewings and said nothing about the rest; it offers to show all of them.

title: The same shelf at either address
items: An owner with a key of their own was that person in a browser from outside the house and somebody else on their own network: the library was told the owner's viewing belonged to the machine rather than to them. Continue watching is now the same shelf whichever address it is reached at, and on the television as well.

title: The copy carries the app as well
items: The machine that keeps copies mirrors the app itself: half-hourly it asks what the house is running and takes it if that is newer, so a phone that reaches the copy is offered the current app rather than whatever that machine's installer happened to carry. What arrives is checked for being an app at all before it replaces anything.

title: One person, one history
items: Whoever owns the machine can watch under a key of their own - the invitation they use on the television and away from the house - and then that is who they are on every screen, this one included. One person had two Continue watching shelves, two watchlists and two rows on the figures page.
The people page shows that person once, marked as you, rather than as a viewer and an owner side by side.

title: What went out, and as what
items: Data sent, month by month and year by year, in the watch log: what people watched and what the machine keeping copies took, in rows of their own. Nothing is counted in both - added together the two answer no question worth asking.

title: The night server says what it is
items: A viewer who lands on the machine that keeps copies is told so, in the browser and in the app: which server it holds copies from, and what of theirs it was asked to keep - what they were part-way through, their watchlist, the next few of their shuffle. A short shelf with no explanation reads as a library that has broken.

title: A dot for what the other machine holds
items: The following server says what it actually has, by this library's own numbers, and a green dot appears on those posters in the browser and in the app. Not what it was asked to keep: a copy that stopped half way is not a copy.
The two buttons for what is kept for each person saved the setting and looked exactly the same afterwards - they had no colour for on.
An address for this machine from outside is taken as typed, with or without http:// in front of it.

The places come with the films. The machine keeping copies is told where each viewing had got to, and hands back what was watched on it, so Continue watching is the same shelf on both - and a film opened after the server has gone to bed carries on rather than starting again.
Casual play is a third thing that can be kept for a person, with its own hours: what the shuffle would put on next, in the order it would put it on.
A file on its way to the machine keeping copies reads as syncing, under that machine's name, rather than as somebody watching a film in another room.

title: The evening moves to the other machine
items: A film whose server goes off carries on from the machine that keeps copies, at the second it had reached - in the browser and in the app. The viewer added one address and is never asked for another.
That machine numbers its own library, so the title is asked for by what it is - a programme, a season and a number, or a title and a year - rather than by a key that means nothing there.
The Test buttons are green while the two machines are in touch, on both sides, without anybody pressing them.

And back again on its own: the server with the library on it is tried about once a minute, and the shelves return to it the moment it answers. A film already playing from the copy is left where it is rather than cut a second time.
The tray opened a browser at 8765 whatever port the server had been set to, which on a second machine is the wrong address. It reads the setting.

The router was never found from a machine with a virtual switch on it: the search for it went out of whichever card the routing table preferred. It is sent from the one facing the house, and opening the port works again.
A folder of copies nothing scans is a folder nobody can watch: the cache joins the library when it is set.

Reach it from the house is green when it is actually working, and says so when it is not: a rule written for a network Windows calls public is on and shut at the same time. There is a button to call the network private, and the switch turns the rule off again as well as on.

title: Test the pair, and see what the cache holds
items: Both halves have a Test button. On the server it knocks on the machine that follows it; on that machine it asks the server a real question with the address and key as they stand, and says which of the two is wrong when nothing answers.
The following server shows what it is holding: gigabytes against the cap, a bar, the number of files, and what is left on that disk.

title: A film that loses its server picks itself up
items: A page whose stream ended in the middle - which is what replacing the server looks like from a browser - opens it again where it was, up to six times, rather than sitting still with the film on screen.

The browser reports what the picture is actually doing rather than what it was last told: a page that came back with a film in place and was never played said it was playing for as long as it stayed open.
And the server no longer believes it: a client that reports the same second for three quarters of a minute is recorded as paused.
Settings could not save a following server: the server ran into a name it did not have while writing down which machine it is.

title: This computer, read as separate things
items: This computer was one box holding five unrelated subjects. It is now a card each: the computer itself, this server's code, following another server, add-ins, and a word to the house.
This server's address and key are shown outright, with Copy beside them, instead of appearing only after a button is pressed.
The port sits with the code that carries it, and the follower settings are grouped under how much to keep and when this machine is the one awake.

title: This computer opens at once
items: This computer opened a second and a half after it was asked for, because asking Windows about the firewall rule starts PowerShell: the answer is kept for five minutes, and the tab no longer waits for the version check either.

title: Every season on the casual shelf
items: A series marked for casual watching showed one season in the app instead of all of them: season cards are named after the programme, and the app was taking two cards with the same name for the same thing.

title: Somewhere to watch when this server is off
items: A server that follows this one tells it where it can be reached, and the app writes that address down. When this server does not answer, the app asks the other machine instead and the evening carries on from the copy.
The browser remembers the address too, and names it when a request finds nothing there.
The following server takes the house's invitations, so a guest reaches the copy with the link they already have.
Another server in the settings says which machine is following this one, and where.
This server's port is a setting: two Palladiums in one house are one router forwarding two ports, the library on 8765 and the machine keeping copies on 8764. Taken at the next start.
Setting up a follower is one line: Copy setup line on the server, Paste setup line on the machine that follows it - the address and the key together.
The follower's address from outside can be set by hand, for one that does not sit behind the same router.
The app offers the copy's address in Servers, so a guest can add it without being told the port.
The machine keeping copies appears in Servers like any other, tagged cache backup, and is added by itself when the server names it.
Settings has what to do with several servers: their libraries together on one shelf, one server at a time, or a shelf for each group. Groups are picked from a list of the ones already named.

title: Lobby
items: The lobby lists who is on the server and what each has playing, above the conversation - the screens that have asked the server for anything in the last five minutes. Local callers only.
The app's Watch party panel has both rooms: Lobby with that list, and Party while one is running. An invitation appears there with Join and No.
The watch party is a tab in the browser rather than a box in the corner: lobby, party and invite as three screens of one page.
The lobby lists one line per screen. It showed a line per address and build, so a phone that had updated twice appeared three times.
A screen is named by its address, or by the name on the invitation when the viewer is a guest. What kind of device it is says nothing about who is watching.
Only people who are here can be invited: the list was every invitation ever made.

Addresses are shown to the owner only. A guest sees who is in the lobby and who is talking, never where they are: an address identifies a machine and, in a house, a person. Anybody the server cannot name is "a screen in the house", and a guest is not offered screens to invite by address - only the other guests.
Casual tab, television: down from the last row of posters no longer jumps back to the Casual play button. The grid refuses the exit while there are rows below it, as it already did going up.
The server-version bar can be reached with the remote and has a button that clears it. It still goes on its own after twelve seconds, unless it holds the focus.
A chat line addressed to one screen now reaches only that screen in the lobby too. The lobby ignored the address and gave every line to everybody.

A report that disagrees about casual watching starts a new watch-log row instead of extending the old one. A row was being extended with its first answer kept, so the log read casual while a progress row was written underneath it.
A progress row written while a casual viewing of the same title is open is noted in debug.log with the screen, client and build that sent it.
A guest can open their collections in the browser. The shelves are the viewer's own, like the watchlist beside them, but the path was not on the list a guest may read and every request was refused.

English is the soundtrack that plays when nobody has chosen one. A release with a dub in front of it started on the dub, because ffmpeg and the player both take the file's first track; the server now names the English one - never a commentary - and the app, the browser and the encoder all start on it. The track list marks it as playing instead of marking the first.
A guest can try a collection rule before saving it, and read which build drew their page. Both were refused: the test ran through /collections/test, which was not on the list a guest may write to.

A file under a season folder is an episode, in a mixed folder as much as in a series one. A ripped series in a download folder became one film per episode: the loose reading only ran for folders already marked as television.
Settings, Library: Read the filenames again. It re-reads every name with today's rules without downloading or probing anything, which is what a scan cannot do because the files have not changed.
A subtitle file beside a video is named by its language first, then whatever else the file name says. One with nothing else read as "sv.srt" in the menu.
The app opens the subtitle in the language the viewer chose on the server, not the one the device is set to. A tablet in English showed English subtitles to somebody whose setting said Swedish.

Reading the filenames again keeps the items already identified. A title matched an existing item only by its exact spelling, so a name from a file - without the apostrophe the catalogue spells it with - made a second, unidentified item and left the first with no files. Punctuation and & against and are now ignored in that comparison.
Marking a whole season or programme watched or unwatched asks first, and says how many episodes it covers. Unwatched forgets where each was left, and one press did it with nothing to undo it.

Full screen in the browser no longer takes the page down on Safari. The element there has no requestFullscreen at all, and calling it threw where a refused promise was expected; it now uses whichever spelling the browser has, or the iPhone's own player.
A settings write that cannot swap the file in - the scanner holding it open - waits longer and, failing that, writes in place. Six tries at 50 ms was not enough and the write was thrown away.

Subtitles can be written from the soundtrack. The button sits under the languages in the download list, in the app and in the browser, and writes the language chosen there. The file is named ai-gen and the list shows it as "Swedish ai-gen", so it is never mistaken for one a person wrote. It runs one at a time on the server's graphics card and takes a few minutes per hour of film; Swedish from English speech uses a second model for the translation.
The row that writes a subtitle from the sound carries the same white ring as the rows above it when the remote is standing on it.
A subtitle written from the sound is turned on as soon as it is ready, on the screen that asked for it.

The soundtrack is decoded with ffmpeg before it is listened to. On one container the model read fifteen seconds of a twenty-two minute episode and stopped, and the subtitle came out with a single line in it.
The speech model is kept as plain files in Palladium's own folder. The cache it downloads into is a tree of links, and the server could not follow them.

A subtitle being written from the sound can be stopped. The row says "Stop writing it down" while it runs, and the browser has a stop beside the percentage; the worker and the ffmpeg reading the soundtrack both go.
While the soundtrack is being decoded the line says how many minutes it has read. On a machine busy transcoding for other screens that step takes minutes, and it looked like nothing was happening.

The subtitle worker runs from Palladium's data folder, not from the program folder. Python puts a script's own directory first on its path, so it was importing the server's compiled modules and holding them open - which is what made the next install stop and ask for an application to be closed.

The worker is started without the server's own PYTHONHOME and PYTHONPATH. They pointed at a runtime that is not the one doing the work, and the job failed at the translation step saying a package was missing that was installed all along.

Writing a subtitle from the sound is offered for English and Swedish only. The model hears any language but can translate into English alone, and Swedish comes from English through a second one; the rest were an offer of a refusal.
A silent install starts the server again afterwards. It replaced a running server and left nothing running.
The row says the language and "ai-gen completed" once one has been written for that file, with "press to write it again" underneath. It went on offering to make the one that was already there.
The percentage appears without anybody pressing anything: the list asks every four seconds, so a job started before it was opened, or from another screen, shows itself.

A subtitle being written from the sound can be watched while it is still being written. The file is rewritten as the words arrive, and the server serves it the way it serves a track being lifted out of a film - marked partial, so the player asks again as the picture nears the end of what it holds.
The track is turned on as soon as there is something in it, rather than when the whole film has been heard.
The film is heard in ten-minute stretches rather than decoded whole first. The first lines are written within a minute instead of after twenty, and each stretch is added to the file as it is done.

Pressing the button closes the list and goes back to the film. How far it has got is said over the picture until there are words on screen, and the track comes on by itself as soon as there is a first line in it.
The button that stops it says "Stop generation".

The soundtrack is read once, in order, while the model works through what has already arrived. Seeking into the file for every stretch made the disk read it again each time: three minutes of work for seven minutes of film.
A subtitle being written is put on the moment it has a line in it, whatever else is showing - including when the film was started from the page after the writing began.
A failure is reported only against the film it happened to. The list showed the last failure whatever it was about, and while a new one was running.

A film playing while a subtitle is being written for it says so over the picture and turns the subtitle on when it arrives. It was waiting for the title, which is only fetched when a panel is opened, so during plain playback it waited for something that never came.

A line is cut where the words are spoken rather than where the model stopped listening. Cues averaged nine seconds on screen and one ran four minutes, which reads as subtitles that do not match the film.
In the browser, a film being watched while its subtitle is written says how far along it is and turns the subtitle on when it arrives, as the app does.
The percentage belongs to the film it is being written for. Opening another title showed that film's progress against this one.
The line under the ai-gen row is written in the colour a note is written in.

Asking what the subtitle machine is doing is answered at once. It used to start a Python and import the whole speech library to find out whether the work could be done at all - on every request, from every screen with the list open - which took the better part of a minute on a busy machine and held up everything behind it, including starting a new one.

In the browser, the green tick is for a subtitle that has been watched through and proved. A file whose name matches the video was given one too, which is a different claim: it says where the subtitle came from, not that it fits.
A subtitle written from the sound is called completed only when it reaches the end of the film. One that stops well short says so instead: it is still being written, or it was stopped part way.

Asking a subtitle to be put in step no longer fails when another one arrives beside the film. Files there are addressed by their place in the list, and one written while the film played moved every place after it.

Settings, This computer: Add-ins. The speech model that writes subtitles from the sound and the translation model that turns English into Swedish are listed with what each is for, what it takes on disk, and a tick to turn it on. Neither ships with Palladium - together they are eight gigabytes - so each is fetched when it is wanted and can be removed again.

One server can follow another. Settings, This computer, Another server: give it the address of the server with the library on it and the key that server hands out, and this one copies whatever that house is watching while it is still on.

A series is copied ahead by the hours set there, so finishing an episode after the other machine has gone to sleep still finds the next one. Copies are kept in a folder of your choosing, inside a disk limit, and the oldest go first - never the one being watched.
A key for a following server is made in the same place. It is an invitation like any other and can be revoked; only a key marked this way may ask what the house is watching.

The following server has night hours of its own - from 22 to 8 by default - and the server it follows says when it goes to sleep. From an hour before that, and through the night, the follower keeps a copy of everything anybody is half-way through, not only what is playing at that moment.
How far ahead a series is copied is set two ways: a number of episodes and a limit in hours. Whichever runs out first stops it.

Settings: the Invite tab is now Users, with two halves. Invite makes and revokes links as before; Users lists everybody who watches here and, for each, whether a following server keeps what they are in the middle of and what they mean to watch. Off for everybody but the owner of the machine: a house with six guests would otherwise ask the other server to hold the whole library.

The Users half says what each person costs: how many files and how many gigabytes a following server would keep for them, and how much of that is half-watched against how much is on their list. The dear ones can then be turned off knowingly.
Stopping a subtitle being written is red in both clients. It throws away what has been done, and read as an ordinary link.

Writing a subtitle no longer fails at the first step. Copying the result beside every copy of a film was written with an import inside the same function that already had one at the top, which makes the name local to the whole of it - so the job died before it began, saying nothing useful.

Asking for a subtitle while one is being written says Queued, and shows how far the one in front has got. One is written at a time - the card cannot do two - and the wait is now visible rather than looking like nothing happened.
A subtitle job that fails takes its worker with it. One that died half way left the process running and the server waiting on it, and everything that asks what is being written waited too.
Friends moved into Users, beside Invite and Users: whose libraries appear here is the same subject as who watches here.

A film no longer starts over and over when its subtitle arrives. Turning the new track on restarts the film with it, and the player that came back found the same job still running and turned it on again - once a second for as long as the writing lasted. It now sees that the track it would switch to is the one already showing, and stops following once it is on.

Each invitation shows its five-character code on the invitations page, with what to do with it: /i/CODE/open opens the library in a browser, /i/CODE.apk fetches the app. The code is derived from the invitation, so it survives a restart and dies when the invitation is revoked.

A subtitle that is still empty when it is turned on is asked for again rather than given up on. One being written from the sound has nothing in it for the first minute, and the player took that for a subtitle with no lines and drew none for the rest of the film.

A subtitle being written says which title it belongs to, so a screen watching that film knows it is theirs without comparing file names. A page that started before the subtitle existed then reads the title again and the track appears in the list.

Asking for a subtitle that is already being written no longer stops the server answering about subtitles at all. The answer to "already" is the state of the work, and reading that took a lock the asking already held - so the two waited on each other and every request about a subtitle file waited with them.

A server can be a cache for one person on somebody else's server. Give it your own invitation instead of a follower key and it keeps what you are in the middle of and what is on your watchlist - only those, and nothing of anybody else's in that house. The page says whose viewing it is keeping.

A subtitle written from the sound is put on where the film is, not where it began. Changing a track on a picture with subtitles burned into it needs a fresh stream, and one started before the player knew its own position began the film again; it now waits for the position and carries on from there.

The browser says how far a subtitle has got every twenty seconds while it is being written, instead of once. The message came after reading the title again, which on a slow line can fail - and the failure ended the watching, so nothing was said after the first time.

A following server takes only films. The machine it follows names each file, and a name is a place: anything with folders in it, anything hidden, and anything that is not a film or a subtitle is refused, and what lands must be inside the folder that was chosen for it.
What arrives has to begin the way a film begins. A program named .mkv is deleted rather than kept, and a file that keeps coming after the size it was said to be is abandoned.

Every file offered to a following server carries a mark - its size and both ends, hashed - and the copy is checked against it. One that arrived changed, short, or substituted for another film of the same length is deleted rather than kept, and a copy already here is trusted only while it still matches.

Subtitles can be fetched, and written from the sound, without starting the film: "Get subtitles" sits at the foot of the subtitle menu on a title's own page in the browser, where the app has had Download in its subtitle panel all along.
The subtitle panel in the player says how far a subtitle being written for this film has got, and how long the wait is if it is behind another one.
The container carries the following-server and subtitle machinery, and the compose example mounts a disk for the copies it keeps.

Download at the foot of the subtitle menu works on a title's own page. The list was written for a film that is playing and had nothing to read when nothing was; it is now handed the title it is about.

The app has the subtitle language in its own settings, under Subtitles with the rest of them, for everybody who watches - not only in the list of subtitles to download. It is kept by the server, so a television and a browser give the same answer.
