Settings, Performance: what this computer is doing that anybody would feel - the graphics card and how hard it is working, films being encoded and for how many screens, a subtitle being written and what is waiting behind it, the library being read, and copies being taken for another server.

Game mode, in the same place. With it on, no subtitle is written and one running is stopped, the library is not read, and a following server takes no copies. Films already playing carry on: somebody is watching them.

Asking for a subtitle to be written shows it as the chosen one at once, with the number on it: "Svenska ai-gen (writing... 23%)" in the list, and the same said at the top of the app's subtitle panel. As soon as the first stretch is written it says ready to play - ten minutes of film is enough to start on, and the rest arrives while it plays.

Game mode says what it holds back, and one button applies it: writing subtitles, reading the library, copying for another server, and - if it is ticked - encoding for a screen. Encoding is left alone unless asked, because stopping it turns somebody's film off.

A subtitle being written appears in the Show list of the film it belongs to, as the chosen one, and says whether there is yet enough of it to start: the first ten minutes are, and the rest arrives while it plays.

Lines are cut where the words are, not where the model stopped listening: a segment with no word timings has its text shared out by length, every line ends before the next one starts, and none is held longer than six seconds. Some lines were coming up early and staying until they were spoken; one ran for four minutes.

A subtitle still being written from a film's sound cannot be put in step until it is finished. It covers the first stretch and no more, and sliding that against the whole film finds agreement where there is none - one such measurement put a film sixty seconds out. Finished, it is measured like any other.
Asking for a subtitle from a title's page closes the list and leaves the film in front of you. When there is enough of it to start, the app says so and puts the remote on Play.

The entry that stands in for a subtitle being written is never sent as a track. It was, which is why a film would not play and said it could not find the file, and it is taken out of the list when the writing ends.

The subtitle box on a title's page says a subtitle is being written from the sound, how far along it is, and "ready to play" the moment there is enough to start. Choosing another subtitle in the meantime settles it: that one is what plays, and the writing only says its piece.

Asking for a subtitle to be written puts it in the subtitle list as a choice of its own, already chosen: "Written from the sound - 23%, not yet enough to start", then "ready to play". Choosing anything else unchooses it, and when the file exists it becomes the real track under its own name - so Play uses it.
Off says off while a subtitle is being written. The box was reporting the writing over the top of a choice to have none.
Coming out of the subtitle panel puts the remote back on the box it was opened from, not at the top of the page.
The subtitle panel says what is chosen when the choice is one still being written. It said Off, which is the opposite of the truth.

Pressing Play with a subtitle that has no lines yet says so, and starts without it on the second press - not with whichever subtitle the language would have picked. The one being written comes on by itself as soon as there is something to draw.
A downloaded update waits to be installed rather than installing itself the instant the last byte arrives. The button says "Install" and wears a white ring; pressing it replaces the app.

A subtitle chosen before pressing play is not overruled by one being written. Choosing English while a Swedish one was being made and pressing play gave Swedish; now only a film started with no subtitle, or with the one being written, has it turned on when it arrives.

A control the remote is put on by name wears its white ring. Focus asked for that way can land on the group around a control rather than the control itself, and the subtitle box came back grey with no ring on it.

A subtitle being written can be chosen from the player's own subtitle list, before it exists. A film playing with none then has them the moment there are enough to read; one playing with none that nobody chose stays as it is.
The subtitle being written is offered in the player's list whatever else is showing, so it can be chosen at any point during a film.
How far it has got is said over the picture only to somebody who asked for it. A number in the corner of a film nobody asked to subtitle is noise.
Choosing the subtitle being written while another is showing turns that one off until there is something to read. It was the one that was asked for, so nothing else stands in for it.

One entry in the list, not two: the subtitle being written is offered only while there is no file for it. Once there is, the track itself is the entry - a film with a half-written subtitle was listing both.

Starting a film on the second press, with a subtitle that is not ready, carries that choice into the film: it says so, plays without subtitles, reports how far the writing has got, and turns it on as soon as there is enough to read.

A subtitle being written comes on for whoever asked for it and for nobody else. A film showing Off keeps showing nothing, and one showing English keeps showing English; the written one waits in the list to be chosen.

The player lists one subtitle where there is one subtitle. It decided whether the written file existed from a copy of the title read before it did - and in a film that copy is fetched only when a panel is opened, so it never saw the track and offered the placeholder beside it. It now reads the title as it stands, and drops the placeholder when the writing ends.

Choosing a language in the list of subtitles to download no longer changes the language every film is chosen in. It says which subtitles that list shows, and which one would be written from the sound; the standing answer is set in Settings, Subtitles, and looking for a Swedish subtitle once was turning it Swedish for good.

A film that will not encode is tried once on the processor before anybody is told it cannot be played. The card can be full - a subtitle being written from a film's sound holds eight gigabytes of it - and it then refuses to start with very little to say.
The browser goes on following a subtitle being written. It was reading a name that belonged to another part of the page, and stopped at the first look.
The settings page kept asking how the scan was getting on even when the server did not answer, instead of stopping with an error.

title: Casual flag on every report
items: Choosing a subtitle, choosing a soundtrack or opening another copy restarts the stream in a new activity, and those three restarts did not carry the casual flag. Every later report from that playing, including the last one, then read as an ordinary watching - which wrote a progress row and put the title in Continue watching. All restarts now carry it.

The server no longer assumes a playing is still casual when a report omits the flag. What the client reports is what is recorded, so the watch log and Now playing show how something was actually watched.
On the Casual tab, pressing down from the tabs lands on the Casual play button instead of the shelf below it.

title: Version numbering
items: Two builds were released as 0.17.25, the second with a fix the first did not have. A version number now moves whenever a build is made, so a running server reports what it actually contains.

title: Subtitle sync, casual playback, watch party naming
items: Subtitle sync no longer fits a drift to windows that matched nothing. A subtitle cut for another edit gave offsets of +23s, +28s, -96s across the film with under 10% of speech matched, and a straight line through that was saved as a 0.6% drift with a 29.7s offset. A fit is kept only when the windows behind it matched.

Casual playback no longer appears in Continue watching. Every progress report carries a casual flag; one report arriving without it wrote a progress row, which is what Continue watching is built from. The server now treats the title as casual for 15 minutes after the last flagged report.
Invitations moved from the top bar into Settings, beside Servers.
The subtitle timing control reads "Timing offset" when a correction is already applied, and names it: static, drift or steps.
The server update button in the app shows "Updating…" while the server restarts, then reports the version that came back.
The notice about a new server version no longer has a dismiss button; it clears itself after 12 seconds.
The app calls the chat panel Watch party, as the browser does.

title: Watch party
items: Chat requires a watch party. With none running, reading returns nothing and writing is refused; joining is implicit on reading, and ending a party clears its messages.
Party messages appear in the bottom right corner of the picture, newest at the bottom, five at most, each removed after 10 seconds.
The subtitle panel points at Settings - Library - Episode numbering when a season's files are numbered differently from the database.
The browser box has three screens: a lobby open to everyone on the server, the party itself, and an invite screen that searches the library and asks chosen screens or guests to watch a title.
Watch parties can be turned off per viewer in Settings - Library. Off means the server sends nothing to that screen; server notices still appear.

title: Addressed messages
items: Messages reach the app: party lines appear over a playing film, named for the sender, and the Watch party button above the shelves opens the conversation.
A message carries its sender - a guest by their invitation name, the owner by a name they supply.
A message can be addressed: no address means every screen on the local network, an address means that screen only, "all" includes viewers outside the house.

title: Chat and notices
items: Server notices appear over a playing film, in the same overlay used by subtitle sync, for 10 seconds.
An update offer names the build number when both sides carry the same version name, instead of reading "0.17.21 is available - you have 0.17.21".
Chat box in the browser: one room for the server, held in memory for the session, delivered over a held connection rather than polled.

title: Notices, quality panel, server updates
items: The quality panel fits a phone: smaller type and tighter rows below 600dp, where "20 Mbit at most" at 18sp did not fit a 160-point column.
The Update button for the server works against an older server that does not report whether the client is on the local network; the server refuses the install itself when it is not.
Skip is shown only when there is a version to skip or a skip to lift.
The app reports when the server it is connected to has been replaced, naming the new version.
Settings - This computer can send a line to every screen on the network, shown across the top of the app for 10 minutes or until dismissed. Held in memory only.
Notices are pushed, not polled: the client asks with the id it holds and the server holds the answer open until there is something to send.

title: Watched, rolled up, and updated from the room
items: An episode is marked watched only when it was watched. The resume point alone said so, which meant skipping to the end - or pressing previous from near it - marked it and moved the series on past an episode nobody saw. How long the player actually sat there is asked as well, from the watch log; a viewing with no log behind it is taken at its resume point as before.

Right along a season's episodes stays in the row. A lazy row composes only what is on screen, so pressing right at the last visible episode found nothing there and focus jumped to Mark all watched, where left and right did nothing.
Go to show on an episode opens the season it is in, standing on that episode, rather than the series with its row of season posters.

The server can be updated from the app and from the browser, by anybody on the same network as it: Settings says which build the server is running and offers the new one when there is one. A screen away from home is told what is running and nothing else - it cannot see what happens next, and the machine it would be restarting is not in front of anybody.

Captions written to roll up the screen are flattened into what is new in each cue. Live captioning writes a line and carries it into the next cue with another under it, which as WebVTT reads as the next line of dialogue appearing long before it is spoken - one cue held from twelve seconds to sixty-eight while the room is silent. Each cue now keeps its own line, ends where the next begins, and stands no longer than eight seconds. A written subtitle file is left exactly as it is.

title: Asked both ways, and no key to update
items: A server updating itself needs no beta key. The key hands the installer to somebody new; an update that stops the day a key expires is one nobody can rely on. The gate answers /build without one, and the key field is gone from the update panel.

A hash match whose name says which episode it is stopped being treated as one for another release. Subtitle sites name episodes their own way, so the right file for an episode can share not one word with the release it belongs to and was being marked and pushed down for it.

A renumbered season is asked for under both numbers - ours and the one the release carries - because subtitle sites are numbered both ways by different uploaders. What the second search finds is offered first among candidates that are equally this episode, and a candidate that is plainly another episode still sinks.

title: Numbering, said and answerable
items: Subtitles for this film says when the release numbers the episodes differently from the season - "file numbers +1" beside the heading. The scanner files them by title, so the number in the name and the number on the screen disagree by that much and nothing is wrong. App 0.16.16.

Settings - Library lists every season whose files count the episodes differently from the database, with how far apart they are and how many files say so. Auto leaves it to the scanner, which puts each episode on the number its own title says; Follow the files takes the number out of the filename instead. A season set to follow the files is left alone by later scans.
The subtitle panel is named for what is playing - "Subtitles for this episode" when it is one - and the browser says the numbering shift beside the heading the way the app does. App 0.16.17.

Asking the tray icon about updates answers beside the icon as well. Windows shuts the menu the moment an item is pressed and it cannot be held open, so the answer was hidden until the menu was opened again.

title: The update outlives the program it replaces
items: Install it wrote its steps into one command line and handed them to a shell started from the server - and the third of those steps kills the server. The shell went with it, so the installer was never reached: both programs stopped and nothing was replaced. The steps are written to a file now, started by a shell that exits at once, and the installer keeps a log in the temp folder.
The beta key saved on a server shows in its own box: /update never sent it back, so the field stood empty and read as "no key here".

An edit form left open on one collection followed you to the next one. It is drawn for one shelf and saves that one, so the next Save would have written the old shelf's name over the new one. Leaving a shelf closes it.

A collection holding both films and television is drawn as two rows, Films then Series, each in the order the sort asks for. One grid ordered by year put a season of the programme between two of the films.

Copying an invitation link worked only on a page opened from localhost or over https. Everywhere else the browser has no clipboard to write to and the button threw, so nothing was copied and nothing was said. It selects the field and copies the old way when the new one is not there.
The figures page answered 500 when an invitation held something other than a name: the name is a key in that reckoning, and a list cannot be one. Everybody's hours were lost to one bad record.
Two places in the player read the film's details before there were any - the version list and the subtitle list, both drawn on the way in.
Air between the shelves on the front page: half a line of the heading's own type above the gap they had, so a row reads as having ended before the next one starts.

A title spelt as the release spelt it is still a film. A name misspelt by whoever packed it found nothing at TMDB, so the film sat in the library with no poster and no plot and was never asked about again. When a name finds nothing, the beginning of it is asked for in shortening steps and the year decides which answer it is - and nothing is taken without a year to judge by.
"Library settings" in the tray icon opens Settings, not the front page. The link names the screen it wants - /#settings/library - and the page follows it; #reports works the same way.

The tray icon asks about builds by itself, every ten minutes and once at startup, so the line names the build waiting to be taken instead of reading "Check for updates" whether or not there is one. When there is nothing to take it says so and says it can be asked again.

Subtitles for this film: Download and the tick that fetches the next episode's subtitle sit together on the left, and Close is at the far right - it is not one of the things done on that panel and beside them it read as one. App 0.16.15.

title: Knowing what a file is, and what is in it
items: The file name above the subtitle list is set in the same face and size as the names below it. Monospace at the same size draws visibly larger than the sans beside it, which is not what "same size" looks like. App 0.16.14.

Identification asks the year before popularity. TMDB answers in the order most people looked things up, and the first answer was taken: a short title came back under the sequel that repeats it, every time. The exact title and the year beside it in the file name are asked first now. Rescanned against a corrected library: 985 of 996 films with a year in the name agree, against 974 before, and twenty titles were wrong that are now right.

A switch for fetching subtitles ahead, above automatic sync in Settings → Subtitles. Five minutes before an episode ends the subtitle the series settled on is fetched for the next one; it always did this and there was no way to say no. Owner's setting - it is their OpenSubtitles allowance and their disk.
Auto-next was off for anybody whose settings held a null for it. The key had been written empty and the default behind it was never reached, so the next episode stopped following this one.
Versions moved under Watch log as a second screen of that tab, and Colour moved from Subtitles to Library.

A file whose probe failed was recorded as probed. ffprobe was never actually run: it was derived by replacing "ffmpeg.exe" in the path of ffmpeg, and WinGet's shim is called ffmpeg.EXE - so ffmpeg itself was run with ffprobe's arguments, answered nothing, and every file scanned since had no codecs recorded. A file with no codecs cannot be shown to play directly, so all of them were transcoded. ffprobe is found beside ffmpeg whatever its case, and a probe that fails on a file touched in the last day is tried again next scan.

title: One press updates it
items: Check for updates in the tray icon, or Install it in Settings, now does the whole job: it stands the server and the icon down, runs the installer, and starts the new program. It used to hand the installer a machine that was still running the very files it had to replace, so the install stopped on a locked libcrypto-3.dll with nobody there to answer.

A newer installer already on this machine is offered before the site is asked. Building one leaves it beside the web client, where /server hands it out - so a build made here can be taken by pressing the same button, with no key, no download and no waiting for the site to publish.

title: What everything here is running
items: Settings → This computer opens with Versions: this server's build, the build the page in front of you was served from, and every app that has asked this server for anything today - what kind of screen it is, which build, its address and when it last spoke. The app has always named itself in a header; the page now does the same, so a tab left open on last week's build is told apart from one reloaded since.
Install it sits above that on the same screen, so what is running and what to do about it are one page.

title: A mark that sticks, and a control you can land on
items: Verifying a subtitle by hand did nothing in an installed server. The library read settings.json from beside its own file, which in a build is a read-only program folder rather than the one the server writes to - so a mark made by hand, a hidden track and the release a series had settled on were all read from a file that was not there. It reads the server's own settings now.

The subtitle selector and its list show the whole name over up to three lines, at the size of the file name above them: three downloaded subtitles for one film differ only at the end of the name, which was exactly what a single line cut off.

The tick in the download list is for what has been proved. A name matching the file says where a subtitle came from, not that anybody has watched the film with it, and it carried a tick that meant something else. App 0.16.10.
The server hands out its own installer at /server: somebody on the same network who wants their own copy should not have to go through the beta gate for a file that is already on this machine.

The verify tick stays where it was, beside the subtitle selector. It was not the control that was wrong: a mark made in an installed server was written to one settings file and read back from another, so nothing ever lit up. App 0.16.12.

The subtitle list wraps a release name instead of ending it in dots. The tick after the name was taking the room the end of the name needed, which is the half that says which release it is. App 0.16.13.

title: Where a subtitle sits, and which one to take
items: Zoom fills the panel, so there is no black under the film and the bottom of the picture is the bottom of the television - text set to the bottom of the screen now sits on that edge. It had been lifted twice: once by a bar that is not drawn when the picture is zoomed, and once by the share zoom crops away, which is not on the screen at all.
On a letterboxed film the same setting still puts the text on the film's own bottom edge rather than in the black under it. Web and app. App 0.16.5.

Pressing zoom while a subtitle is on screen moves it with the picture. The cue was placed once and left alone while its text stood, so the line stayed at the old picture edge until the next subtitle arrived. App 0.16.6.

On a phone the text sat under the picture rather than on it. The black was being padded out of the subtitle view to make nought the picture's bottom edge, and the child view that draws the cues keeps the size it was measured at, so the fractions went on being counted off the whole window. The bar is part of the placement now. App 0.16.7.

A subtitle named after the video file itself now leads the download list and says "same name as the file". It is the strongest evidence there is that the timing fits - whoever made it had this release in front of them - and it was being placed below a hash match and below whatever had the most downloads.
The video's own file name sits at the top of the download list and stays there while the list scrolls, so the release names can be compared against it.
Downloading a subtitle turns that subtitle on. It turned on whichever file the library listed last beside the video, which with three of them was rarely the one just taken.
When a search by database id comes back empty, the title is asked for by name before giving up: a remake takes the name and the old id keeps the subtitles. App 0.16.8.

A hash match whose name is for a different release is no longer trusted or called "matches this file". The hash is the file's size and its first and last few kilobytes, and uploaders attach them by hand - a DVDRip and a one-word upload both claimed to be a 1080p BluRay and were offered above the subtitle actually named after the file. They are still listed, marked "hash says this file, name says another", below what agrees with the release. App 0.16.9.

title: The server can fetch its own next build
items: Reports → What is new carries the build this machine is running against the one palladium.video is publishing. When a newer one is out, Install it fetches the installer through the beta gate, checks it against the hash the site published, runs it silently and starts the program again. Settings, invitations and the index are untouched by the upgrade.
A beta key field beside it: the key this copy was downloaded with, used for updates too, so withdrawing a key stops both.
A copy running from source says so and offers no button - there is nothing to replace.

The installer stops asking. It had a folder page that reads as "where are your films" when it means where the program goes, and two questions about starting at sign-in and letting the house in - asked before there was a library to serve, and the second needing an administrator the installer never had. All three are gone; the two settings live in Settings under This computer, where the firewall one can ask Windows properly.
The packaged tray started nothing: it looked for pd-server.py and a Python to run it, neither of which exists in a build, so the icon appeared and vanished. It runs the server beside it now.

On the set, a subtitle placed off the picture hung off the bottom of the panel: the top of the text was placed and the rest was not counted, so the second line of a two-line cue was drawn past the edge. Both placements are told how tall the cue is now, and neither can be pushed off the screen. App 0.16.3.

title: Shaping the casual shelf, and marks that wait for Save
items: Edit on the Casual tab: a cross on every poster, a red wash over what will go, and Save or Cancel. Nothing is written until Save, so a handful of presses can be undone in one.

Taking one season off a programme marked whole did nothing at all - the mark the season was drawn from was never touched, so the shelf put it straight back. The mark above is now broken into its own parts, minus the one taken off: a programme becomes its seasons, a season its episodes.

While a filter is being tested, the tick and cross move a poster between the rows without writing anything. Save keeps the marks along with the rule; Cancel test puts the saved arrangement back. Choosing the collection's poster is not offered mid-test, because that button writes at once.
While a test is on, the rows follow the Include and Exclude boxes as they are typed in, a moment after the last keystroke; an older answer never draws over a newer one.
The manual edit label on a poster is now the way to take that edit back: press it and the rule decides the title again. Staged while a test is on, written at once otherwise.
A collection being looked at no longer carries crosses on its posters. Taking titles out belongs to Edit, where the two rows say what in and out mean.
Edit rows moved onto the first row's line, just left of its See all, instead of sitting in a bar of its own above the page.
The Edit rows box opens at the top right of the page, under the button that opens it, rather than pushing the first row down.
The app has a Collections tab: the shelves as posters with what each holds, and one opens into its titles in release order. Back leads out of a shelf. App 0.16.0.

In the app, a collection carries the same sort as Films and TV, starting at release order oldest first, and two ways to start it: Play takes the first in the order shown, Shuffle draws one out of it. A series opens its page rather than playing blind. App 0.16.2.
In the player, pressing down twice lands on the step forward rather than on the step back, which is the way out of a scene nobody asked for.

title: Continue watching plays, and collections take an exclude rule
items: A card in Continue watching starts the video at once. A film or episode resumes where it was left; a series or season looks up the next episode first. It opens the title page only when there is nothing to play.

A paused player reports every eight seconds, and the watch log extended the viewing on each report, so a film left paused counted as watch time. Paused reports now move the place and the length, not the clock, and a viewing does not start while paused.

A collection's rule has two boxes: Include and Exclude, read the same way - every word in a rule must appear, a bar starts another rule. A title matching any exclude rule stays out whatever the include rules said.

Test filter tries the rule without keeping it: the titles move into the rows it would put them in, washed green for taken and red for left out. The button reads Cancel test while it is on and puts the saved arrangement back.
Searching inside a collection and then pressing the cross puts that collection back on screen instead of the shelf of shelves.

The Casual tab says beside the sort that nothing played there appears in Continue watching. The played tally moved to the right end, beside the count, and + New on Collections sits left of the shelf count.

A tick or cross on a filter collection now records only what the rule does not already say: putting back something the include words catch lifts the strike without pinning it, and taking out something they never caught lifts the pin. Overrides that agree with the rule are dropped when the rule is saved, so a poster is labelled a manual edit only where it really is one.

Settings writes were being thrown away when Windows refused the swap because another reader held the file open - six lost in a day. The swap is retried for a third of a second, and the temporary file is named per process. The same goes for the invitations file.

Excluded while editing shows what the exclude words took out as well as what was struck out by hand, and a title that is where it is by a manual edit says so on its poster. The Holds row reads Episodes rather than Programmes.

Very bottom drew at the top of the window in the browser: the drawn cue layer read 0.99 as a share of the height rather than as the floor step it is. It sits at the bottom of the screen now, and follows the window as it is resized.

Off the picture no longer falls back to another setting. A film that fills the screen has no black under it, and the text stays on the lowest row rather than jumping back onto the picture; a height chosen from the in-picture list that is deeper than the off-picture steps is drawn at the last of them, and switching to Off screen brings the stored height back to it. Web and app both.

title: The tabs stop shuffling
items: The chosen tab is bold, and bold is wider, so pressing one moved every tab to the right of it by a pixel or two. Each tab now reserves the width of its own label in bold, drawn invisibly, and the row holds still: measured at the same eight positions on Home, Films, TV and Watchlist alike.

title: Reports stays on the bar
items: It stepped aside on Films and TV, where the row is already busy. A tab that comes and goes is one nobody can rely on finding, and its count of unread reports is the part worth seeing.

title: The same sort everywhere, and a name of your own
items: The Collections page takes the sort control the rest of the program uses, in place of the three orders it had invented for itself. A collection has a name and the date it was made to sort on, so the orders that ask about a picture leave the shelves as they were made.
A search offers Make collection beside the count of what it found, drawn as the New button on the Collections page, in place of the row of buttons that used to appear above the results.
The watch log and the figures call the owner by name. "You" read as a fourth person standing beside the guests.
Play and Shuffle stand down while a collection is being shaped: the two rows on screen are not an order anything would go on in.

title: Two things said plainly
items: Where an address is shown as an example rather than as this server's own, it reads xxx.xxx.xxx:8765. A made-up address that looks real is read as one to type.
The casual shelf says what it does not do: nothing played from it appears in Continue watching, which is the point of it and was nowhere written down.

title: A collection opens oldest first
items: Released, oldest first, is where a collection starts - a series is watched from its beginning. It keeps that order separately from Films and TV, where Released means newest first and should.
Three examples of the filter syntax sit under the box in italics, which teaches it better than the sentence above them.

title: Search words, and a rule per bar
items: The Words box is called Search words and says what it takes: every word in a rule must appear in the title, so star wars finds only those; a bar starts another rule and a title joins if it answers any of them, so alien | predator takes both.
Measured on this library: alien | predator gathers fifteen titles, and alien vs gathers the two crossovers alone.

title: The sort sits beside the name on every list
items: In a collection and on the watchlist the count stood between the name and the sort. The sort follows the name and the count ends the line, as it does on Films and TV.

title: One sort control for every list of titles
items: The watchlist and a collection carry the same sort as Films and TV - added, released, name, year, quality, with the arrow that turns it round - rather than a set of their own invented for the purpose.
A collection keeps the release order it is sent in, which is how a series reads, and says so beside the control until an order is chosen.

title: An arrangeable front page, and collections that play
items: The front page can be arranged: Edit rows turns any shelf off and moves the rest past each other. The arrangement is the viewer's and the server keeps it, so every screen agrees; the owner can make the one on screen what everybody starts with.

A collection is a filter or a list. A filter keeps looking - anything the library gains that answers its words joins it - while a manual one holds what it is given and nothing else. Either way a title can be struck out by hand.

A collection plays: Play current order takes the titles as they are shown, Shuffle draws an order once so nothing repeats before the shelf is through. The next starts as each one ends, and putting anything else on ends the run.
The titles inside a collection can be ordered by release, by name, by when they were added, or newest first - and that is the order Play current order uses.

title: Each title once while a collection is edited
items: Editing a collection drew everything it holds twice: once in Included and once in the grid the page already had underneath. That grid steps aside while the two rows are up, so every title appears once, in one row or the other.
The collection's own way back is gone; the arrow in the top bar was already pointing at the shelf it was opened from.

title: Collections have a tab, and a face
items: Collections moved off the watchlist and onto a tab of their own, drawn as posters: each takes the poster of the first title it holds, or of whichever one is chosen for it. The number it holds sits in the corner.
A star on any title inside a collection makes that title's poster the collection's own.

Pressing Edit shows both sides at once - Included and Excluded - so a collection can be shaped without searching for anything. The five titles struck out of the Alien shelf sit there ready to be put back.
The chosen order of the collections is remembered in the browser.

title: Collections: one name each, an order, and buttons that look like buttons
items: Two collections cannot share a name, and none can be called Watchlist, which is the name of the shelf itself. A refusal says which name is taken and leaves the form open with what was typed.
New and Edit are drawn as actions - outlined, set apart - rather than as two more collections at the end of the row.
The collections can be listed in the order they were made, by name, or by how many they hold. The choice is the browser's, not the server's.
A collection shown whole no longer carries an Included heading: the name is already above it, and Included only means something against the Excluded a search puts underneath.

title: Clearing the search puts back what was there
items: The cross in the search box, or deleting the last letter, left the results on screen with nothing searched for. It now returns to the tab the search was made from, and to the collection itself when one was open.
Only when the results came from the search: clearing the box while a film's page is open leaves the film where it is.

title: The collection buttons carry the name alone
items: A count on the button read as part of the name - Alien 8 looked like a collection called that. How many a collection holds is said beside the heading when it is open.

title: Included and Excluded
items: The two sections in a collection are called Included and Excluded, in the collection itself and in a search inside one.

title: Building a collection from a search, and editing it with two marks
items: A search on any tab offers to become a collection: a new one whose rule is the words searched for, or every title found added to one that exists.
Inside a collection each poster carries one mark, the same two the Continue watching shelf uses - a cross takes a title out, a tick puts one in.

Searching while a collection is open splits what it finds in two: what the collection already holds above, what it does not below, each with the mark that moves it across. The ordinary search box does this - there is no second one.

title: Collections
items: Named shelves alongside the watchlist, each with a rule: words a title must carry, and optionally films only or programmes only. They sit as a row above the grid and open like a folder.

A rule rarely fits a canon exactly, so a collection also keeps two lists by hand - titles pinned in and titles struck out. Alien on this server matches eleven films by name: four of them belong to another series, and Prometheus belongs but never says so. Pinned and struck out, it comes to seven, in release order.
Collections belong to the viewer, like the watchlist, and a guest keeps their own. Deleting one leaves every film where it was.

title: Two faults off the Errors page
items: Nineteen places wrote settings.json directly instead of through the one function that takes a lock and swaps the file in atomically. Two progress reports arriving at once could collide on the open file, which is the Access is denied recorded three times last night. All of them go through it now.
The subtitle download list read the playing session on every click. Closing the film with the list open left it reading a session that no longer existed. It holds the title it was opened on.

title: The burn-in setting covers casting too
items: The setting gated the pipe a browser plays through but not the playlist a Chromecast plays through, so casting burned a bitmap track whatever it said. Both paths check it now. Verified: under Nobody, a playlist asked with a burn returns the film and the running chain carries no overlay.
The block is called Burn-in transcoding, and says what it costs: the whole film re-encoded for as long as it plays, plus the upload when the viewer is remote.

title: Three settings for burning a bitmap subtitle
items: Everyone, local network only, or nobody. Nobody hides PGS and VobSub tracks from every browser including this machine, which is the setting for a server that should never spend an encode on a subtitle.
Local network only stays the default. A refused track is filtered out of the picker, and a request for one is answered with the film and no subtitle rather than an error.
The Android app is unaffected in all three: it decodes bitmap tracks itself.

title: Plainer wording in the settings
items: The subtitle sync and picture-subtitle settings said what they did in prose rather than in terms. They now name the mechanism: cue times and offsets, PGS and VobSub, re-encode and upload. Buttons read On and Off instead of describing themselves.
Same for the accent note, the watched-hours note, and the two panels in the app.

title: Search by number, and keep the painting at home
items: Subtitles are searched for by the title's IMDb number rather than by its name. A name is parsed at the other end, and a title ending in four digits is read as a year: one film asked for subtitles from the year 2049 and was told there were none. By its number it answers with twenty. 1917, 1984 and 2012 were the same trap.

Picture subtitles are no longer offered to a browser away from home. Painting one into a film is a whole encode for a subtitle, and down somebody else's line it is paid for twice - so the tracks are not offered rather than offered and refused, and the server turns down a request for one anyway. In the house nothing changes, and the app is untouched because it draws them itself.
The setting sits on the subtitle page and belongs to the owner: it is their machine and their line.

title: A burned subtitle never leaves the card
items: Burning a picture subtitle was copying every frame out of the card, mixing a bitmap into it on the processor and pushing it back, for as long as the film ran - 70% of a machine while the card sat at 10. It is all on the card now: the picture stays there, the subtitle goes up to it, and the blend is the card's.

Measured on a 4K scope film with its sound: 0.29 times real time through system memory, 0.98 on the card. And the frame it produces is byte for byte the one the old path produced, so nothing about how the text looks has changed.
Where the ffmpeg in hand has no overlay on the card, the old path stands.

On a film's page the subtitle picker has a row of its own under the file, both words are one width so the two dropdowns start at the same place, each label sits level with the middle of its control, and the watchlist and shuffle marks no longer sit a pixel below the buttons beside them.

title: The subtitle picker was pinned to the floor by its own name
items: On a film's page the label said Subtitles up in the row and the dropdown sat at the bottom of the window, wherever the page was scrolled. The layer that draws subtitles over a film has been called subs since the beginning, and the stylesheet fixes that name to the foot of the screen - the picker had taken the same name, so the browser applied the rule to a dropdown. It has a name of its own now.
The copy and the subtitle share one line and shrink to fit rather than one dropping below the other; below 700 points across they stack, which is the width where sharing stops being kind.

title: The two choices on a film's page share a row
items: Which copy and which subtitle sat on a row each, which left the subtitles at the foot of the page under the summary. They are the same kind of decision made at the same moment, so they are one row now, each with a word in front of it - two bare dropdowns read as something somebody forgot to finish.
"Subtitles off" in a list labelled Subtitles is now just "Off", and a picture track says "burned in" rather than explaining itself in five words.

title: A picture subtitle is not a CPU encode
items: The browser's subtitle list called a picture track "burn-in, uses CPU", which was true when the encoder was software. The film is encoded on the card; what the processor still does is lay the picture over each frame.

title: The browser shows the server's version, not the phone's
items: The number beside the name was read from the app's own release, which the browser does not run. The two were one sequence while both were built together and have drifted since. The page carries this server's release now, with the app's version and build date in the tooltip for anybody comparing a phone against a browser.

title: A file that cannot give Dolby is only asked once
items: The first play of a file whose Dolby track comes out empty spends the whole wait discovering it - fifteen seconds before a frame, then a fresh encoder. It is written down now, against the file's size, so every play after that starts on plain sound straight away. Measured on the episode it was found on: 15.6 seconds, then 0.3.
A file replaced by a better rip is asked again rather than judged by what the old one did.

In the browser's Aa panel, a subtitle painted into the picture leaves its face, its colour, its backing and its placement faded - none of them can act on a picture, and the last cannot put it below a frame it is inside. Size and place still work, because the server applies those while painting.

title: DTS goes through to a set that can decode it
items: The app asks the audio chain what it can take - not the box, the chain, so a streamer with no decoder of its own still counts a receiver that has one - and where DTS is answered for, the track goes through untouched. Nothing decoded, nothing re-encoded, and the sound that arrives is the one on the disc.
Where it is not, the AC-3 we make from it stands, and the plain-sound fallback after that.

The burned subtitle geometry is back where it was. I measured a subtitle plane against the picture instead of against itself, on the reasoning that a disc's canvas and a scope picture are different sizes - and made the text enormous on the very film it was meant to fix.

title: The download list is ordered by the release it has to match
items: A subtitle is cut to one release, and the one named after the same release as your file is the one whose timing fits - but the download list was leaving that to the provider's own order. It sorts on it now: the right episode first, then a match on the file itself, then how much of the release the name shares.

A subtitle matched by hash - uploaded against a file byte for byte the same as yours - was being pushed down the list for not spelling the episode's title out in its name, which release names rarely do. It is the right episode by definition, and it leads.

A name that says which episode it is, and says a different one, is no longer treated as this episode however well its words match. Both halves of a two-parter carry the same title, so the second half was passing for the first - and once the release decided the order, it led the list.

title: An episode that would not start
items: One episode never began. Its sound is DTS, so it has to be re-encoded, and on that file the muxer took the AC-3 track and wrote nothing at all - with the delayed header it waits for one it never manages, without it the header cannot be written. The film was fine; nothing ever came out of the encoder.

The wait for a stream's first block is bounded now, so a muxer that will never write is cut off rather than left holding the request open with no answer. And when Dolby produces nothing the film is asked for again with plain sound, which every device takes, before giving up on it.
The episode plays. Its sound arrives as AAC rather than AC-3, which is the trade for having it at all.

title: A colour of your own
items: The accent belongs to the viewer now, not to the server. Choose one in the browser or in the app and it follows you from the television to the phone, because the server keeps it against your name - and nobody else's screens change.
The server's colour is what somebody meets before they have chosen, and there is a way back to it from either place. The owner can still set that default, and only the owner can.
A guest could not reach the colour row at all before; it was the owner's, and it repainted the house.

title: A burned subtitle is sized against the picture, and the menu names it
items: The subtitle plane was scaled by a factor of its own size, and a plane is authored on the disc's canvas - 1920 across on a Blu-ray - while the picture may be anything. On a scope film cropped to 3840 by 1600 that left the text at about half the size the disc drew it. It is measured against the frame it is laid on now, so one number means one size whatever the file is.
The size was also being multiplied by the resize a second time on any film being made smaller, which halved it again.

With a picture subtitle drawn by the device, the subtitle menu said Off while it was plainly on the screen: there is no fetched file behind one of those, and the menu was reading the number off the file's address. It reads what was asked for instead.

title: Aa is locked while the film draws its own subtitle
items: With a picture subtitle on screen the Aa button in the player is faded, and pressing it says why rather than opening a panel whose every control would do nothing. The size and the place of one of those is inside the image, decided when the disc was made.
The timing controls in the subtitle panel were already faded for the same reason; the button that opens the look settings was not.

title: The television draws a picture subtitle itself
items: A subtitle off a disc is a set of images, not text, and until now the only way to show one was to paint it into the film - an encode of every frame, which on a 4K disc runs at half real time and looks like a copy of the film rather than the film. The player decodes those images itself, so the film plays untouched and the words go on top. 315 files here hold nothing but picture subtitles.
Burning is what is left for the cases that cannot draw them: a browser, a television being cast to, or a film already being encoded for its sound or its size.

The timing controls stay in the panel when one of these is playing, faded, with the reason under them: the size, the place and the timing are part of the image. A control that vanishes sends somebody hunting for a setting they think they have lost.

title: A transcode that still looks like the film
items: A device that says it decodes HEVC is sent HEVC, at the size the file is. The h264 ceiling of 1920 across stays for everything else, because that is a real limit on these boxes - but it meant a 4K film was halved to reach a television that would have taken it whole, and next to a direct play the difference is not subtle.
The app asks the device itself rather than guessing, and the answer rides with the request.

title: An encoder that will not start says so
items: A stream is answered only once the first block has arrived. An encoder that refuses to start used to be answered with 200 and an empty body, which a player can only read as a broken container - the fault it reported named the film and told you nothing about the cause. It is a 502 now, carrying ffmpeg's own first complaint, and the same line goes to the Errors page and the log.

That fault was ours: resizing a burned subtitle on the card left hwdownload to negotiate its format with the overlay, the overlay asked for alpha, and a frame on the card cannot be downloaded with alpha. The format is pinned now, and a 4K film with a burned subtitle plays again.
Watched hours count a viewing for no more than the length of what is being watched. A player left reporting made one twenty-minute episode read as thirty-five hours.

title: A dropped stream comes back where it was, and the house's hours
items: When a stream stops arriving the player asks for it again from where it had got to - not from where the player says it is. A player whose stream is pulled away can report nought, and starting again there means watching the first minutes over and over. That is what a restarted server did to somebody all one evening: two hours and twenty-three minutes of an episode, and three and a half minutes of it seen.
Half a minute of clean playing earns the retries back, so a long film survives more than two blips in an evening.

Now playing counts a viewing rather than a socket. A direct play is a run of range requests, each one opening and closing, so the list flickered - a row appearing and vanishing several times a minute while somebody sat still watching. Every connection for one person, title and screen is one row now, and a row is held for half a minute after its last socket closes.
Watched hours for the week, the month and altogether, above the log: how many viewings, how many titles, who did the watching and what took the most time.

title: Every fault lands on the same page
items: The server's own faults were written to stdout, and the server runs without one - so anything that went wrong inside it was lost entirely. They now go to the log with the whole trace and onto the Errors page beside the ones the app and the browser report. The same fault is filed once an hour, so a page asking every few seconds cannot bury the rest.

A request to burn a subtitle that the chosen copy does not hold is refused rather than obeyed. Asking for stream 3 of a file whose only subtitle is stream 2 left ffmpeg with nothing to overlay, and the television reported a container it could not parse. It plays without the subtitle instead.
That is what happened to a 4K film this evening: the copies were reordered while it was playing, so the number the player was holding meant a different file by the time it asked for more.

title: The subtitle chosen by itself is the one cut for the film
items: A subtitle whose last line is spoken after the film has ended belongs to something else, and now goes to the bottom of the list. An episode with two files beside it was opening with the one that ran two and a half minutes past the credits.

And the players take the first file beside the video rather than the last. The server ranks them - proved on this series first, then the one chosen last time - and taking the last undid the ranking every time there was more than one.

title: A 4K film with a burned subtitle keeps up
items: The transcoder was sending a television 4K h264, which these boxes do not decode - they take HEVC and VP9 at 2160 lines and h264 at 1080. A 4K film played straight until a picture subtitle forced an encode, and then stuttered. h264 is now capped to 1920 across, measured on the width because a scope film is 3840 by 1600 and 1600 lines is still 4K wide.

Burning a subtitle now resizes on the card before the frames come down, and scales the subtitle plane by the same amount, so the text keeps its size against the picture. A quarter of the pixels to copy and a quarter to overlay.
The largest file of a title is the one played by default. Ordering by picture height put a 1080p trailer above a 720p feature in the same folder, and the trailer is what got played.

title: The marks on a poster come out from behind it
items: The poster image is on a layer of its own, and everything drawn over it was not - so a positioned mark painted underneath the picture. The 4K badge showed the fault because it was new; the resume bar and the time beside it had been invisible on a card in the browser all along.
Every mark on a poster now has that layer: where it came from, the watchlist star, the shuffle mark, the watched tick, the 4K badge, the progress bar and its time.

title: The 4K badge moves to the corner it belongs in
items: Bottom right on the poster, lifted clear of the progress bar. It was top right in the browser, which is where the watched tick already sits - a finished 4K film drew both in the same place.

title: A year and a category are things to search for
items: Typing a year lists what came out that year, and typing a category lists that shelf - films first, then programmes. Each gets a row of its own under the titles that carry the word, so 1917 still finds the film before it finds the year.
A category is recognised however it is typed: sci fi finds Sci-Fi & Fantasy, doc finds Documentary. Two letters are a word half typed rather than a category, and are left alone.
In the app the same searches work and the results arrive in one list, as they always have.

title: 4K, said on the poster and sorted for
items: A title held in 4K wears a 4K badge on its poster, in the browser and in the app. A series wears it when any season does, which is the reason to pick it off a shelf.
Quality is an order in the sort list, best picture first. Anything nobody has measured goes to the bottom either way round: an unprobed file is unknown, not small.
Searching for 4k, 2160p or uhd lists everything held that big rather than looking for the letters in a title. 20 films and 2 series here.

The measure is the frame, not the height. A scope film off a 4K disc is 3840 by 1600 and reads as less than 1080p by height alone, so it counts as 2160 - which is what it is. That found eleven 4K films this server was not calling 4K.

title: Subtitles are put in step for everyone
items: Automatic subtitle sync is a server setting now, on the subtitle page, and it is on unless it is turned off. It used to be one switch per viewer inside the player, which meant anybody who never opened that panel got nothing - and the measurement is the server's work, not a matter of taste.
It is the default rather than an order: whoever has turned it off for themselves in the player keeps that answer. Everyone else follows the page.
The accounts already on this server were set to follow it once, when the setting was added.

title: The best copy by default, and the one you choose after that
items: A title held more than once opens on its best copy - the list is ordered by picture and rate, so that is simply the first. Choose another and the server remembers it against the title, so the browser, the phone and the television all open on it from then on. Nothing is stored for the best copy, so a better rip added later becomes the default rather than losing to an old choice.
The film's page has the file name under the buttons and the subtitle list under that, each on its own line: a release name is half the width of the page and the subtitle names are wider.

The copy select answered to the same name as the version number in the corner, so pressing play read the wrong element and asked for copy NaN - which the server floored to the first file. Choosing a copy in the browser has never worked until now.
The subtitle list follows the copy. Two files of one film hold different tracks under different numbers, so the list built for one of them named a track the other does not have.
A faint P sits behind the page, under the artwork and under the poster.

title: Choose the copy in the app
items: A title the library holds twice - a 4K copy and a 1080p one, or a remux beside something cut down for a phone - can be chosen between on its page in the app. The browser has had the dropdown all along; the app played the first file and gave no way to reach the other. Each copy is listed by its release name with its size, codec, rate and how many subtitles it carries.

Everything downstream follows the copy: playback, the subtitle list, the tracks the player fetches, and syncing, planning and resetting a subtitle, all of which sent copy zero whatever was on screen. Two files of one episode are out by different amounts, so a measurement taken against the wrong one was wrong.
Back steps through the screens again, as it did before yesterday's release.

title: Three small ones
items: An invitation now says what to do with a Samsung set: the address to type into the television's own browser, which is the whole library signed in as them, and below it the longer route to an icon on the home row - the source, and the plain warning that it needs Tizen Studio and a certificate of their own.

The subtitle panel names the file that is playing. Two copies of the same episode are out by two different amounts, and the release name is the only thing that says which one a subtitle was cut for; finding it meant leaving the player.

On a television, Back at the top of a list goes to Palladium's home rather than out of the program, and leaving takes a second press - with a word first, since dropping a set to its own home screen without warning means finding the app again.

title: Off the picture, the top of the text is what is placed
items: The first row now begins where the picture ends, and a second line - or a line long enough to wrap - grows downwards into the black rather than back over the film. The app anchors the top of the text outright; the browser, which cannot be told to, allows for the rows a long line takes at the width it has.
On the picture nothing changes: the bottom of the text is placed and it grows upwards, which is what a subtitle in a picture should do.

title: On screen, or off it
items: "The film" and "The whole screen" are now "On screen" and "Off screen", which is what the choice actually is: text in the picture, or text in the black below it.

Off screen, the steps run the other way. The first sits as close under the picture as it goes and each one after it is a row further down, which is the direction anybody means by putting the text off the film. They are named for it too - Nearest, One down, Two down, Lowest - rather than Bottom and Just up, which point the wrong way there.
In the app the setting did nothing at all: the subtitles were drawn inside the picture, so there was no black to move into. They are drawn over the whole player now, and both answers work.
Off screen, the whole line clears the picture rather than only its last pixel: the text began at the film's bottom edge, so most of it was still on the picture.
And a step of its own for the very bottom of the panel, whichever way the text is placed - as low as the screen goes, whatever shape the film is.

title: Choosing a track inside the film sticks
items: Only a file beside the video could be remembered. Choosing a track inside the film sent nothing to the server, which reads as "subtitles off" - so the choice was thrown away, the film opened next time as though nothing had been chosen, and a film whose only subtitles live inside it could never be given a preference at all.
A track inside the film is now remembered by its number, as timing corrections and verified marks already were. Both players send it and the menu marks it.

title: Settings remembers the film you came from
items: Stepping aside to Settings or to Reports from a title's page kept no way back to it - the arrow went out and the tabs started afresh, so the only route back to the film was to find it again. Both now keep the page underneath and the arrow returns to it. The library tabs are destinations and still start clean.

title: The subtitle cut for your copy wins by itself
items: Several subtitles beside one episode are usually for different releases, and only one of them was cut for the copy you hold. That one is now chosen for you when nothing has been chosen yet - scored on the release alone, since the programme's name and the episode's number appear in all of them and say nothing about timing.

And when a subtitle cannot be placed against the film, the refusal now proves itself where it can. Another file beside the same episode that does match the release settles it: lines they share that are out by the same amount everywhere mean the file is merely late, and that number is offered. Lines out by anything from -27 to +44 seconds mean it was made for a different edit, and no correction can fit it.

A file that is itself the release's own says so, rather than being called suspect for failing a measurement it cannot pass: an episode that talks without pausing has nothing to line anything up against.

title: A white P on a blue tile
items: The mark is white on a filled blue tile now, rather than blue on near-black - an icon in a launcher row or on a television shelf has to hold its own against whatever is beside it, and a dark tile disappears into the row.

The tile is one step deeper than the accent, #2F6FD0, which puts white at 4.9 to 1 and keeps it crisp at 48 pixels. The blue P on the dark bar inside the program is unchanged - a filled tile up there would be heavy.
Everywhere at once: the app icon and its two older raster sizes, the television banner, the icons the server hands to a browser, and the site.

title: Subtitles arrive before the film has been read
items: A subtitle inside a film had to be lifted out before any of it could be shown, and a container has no index for subtitles - the whole file has to be read. On a 6.6 GB film that was minutes of watching without text.

The first twenty minutes are lifted out on their own, which stops as soon as ffmpeg is past that mark, and the rest is read behind it. Measured on that same 6.6 GB film: text on screen in 13 seconds instead of minutes, and the whole track in hand before the twenty minutes were up.
Both players ask again as they approach the end of what they hold, so the changeover is invisible.
A subtitle fetched by hand that turns out to be identical to one already beside the film is not written twice - the menu was showing the same file under two names.

title: Now playing says what is playing it
items: Each row names the device, what sort of thing it is, and which build is running: "Streamer · Google TV app v0.14.56". A fault reported from a three-week-old build is a different conversation from one on today's, and the answer used to mean opening the watch log to find it.
It holds for somebody paused as well as somebody streaming - the player's own report carries the same two facts as the stream does.

title: Said once, properly
items: The verified notice still came twice: the first report after the credits knows the file that was fetched and the ones after it know the track on screen, so the two records differed and each announced itself. The news is the moment a subtitle goes from unverified to verified, and nothing after that.
Measured: twelve reports through the credits, one notice.

title: Said once
items: The subtitle-verified notice arrived every few seconds until the episode was over. Progress is reported all the way to the end and every report after the credits made the same mark, so every one of them was announced. Only the first is news now; the app also keeps its own count, so a restart in the middle cannot bring it back.

title: Pick the colour
items: Twelve accents on the settings page, and the choice belongs to the server: the television, the phone, the browser and the pages the server puts up before anybody signs in all draw with the one you pick. Every colour on offer carries dark text at 5.7 to 1 or better, so none of them can be chosen into illegibility.
The old gold is in the row, last, marked "don't use this" - it is there so nobody wonders where it went.
The launcher icon keeps the blue - that one is baked into the app when it is built.

title: The tick turns as the credits arrive
items: Nothing verified itself any more, and the reason was blunt: the players report that a subtitle is on, not which one, and a rule added this morning compared that word with the name of the file that had been fetched, found them different and refused. Every automatic verification since then was lost that way.

The reports now name the subtitle - a number for a track inside the film, the release name for a file beside it - so any subtitle can earn its mark by carrying an episode to the end, not only one the server fetched itself.

And the answer to that last report carries the news, so a panel that is open turns its tick green as it happens and the player says so for a moment. It used to appear the next time the panel was opened.

title: Verifying survives a restart
items: When a subtitle came on was held in memory only, so a server restart in the middle of an episode looked exactly like a subtitle chosen at the end: the rule that stops a track picked in the last minute from being credited with the whole film then refused it, however far the episode was watched. On a ten-minute episode the window is three minutes, so almost any restart lost it.
It is written down now, in the settings file, and only when the subtitle changes. A restart picks up where it left off, and a position that cannot be known is treated as unknown rather than as late.

title: A colour of its own
items: The accent was #E5A00D, carried over from what this program started life as. Too close to another media server's for comfort: a dark theme and that colour read as a reskin of it.

It is now #4A90F0, sampled from a poster in the library: the mean of the bright blue on it, nudged up for contrast. Dark text on the accent and the accent as text on the page both come out at 5.8 to 1, comfortably past the 4.5 that counts as readable.
Everywhere at once: the mark, the app icon and the television banner, the tabs and buttons, the setup and sign-in pages the server draws, and the television web app.

title: Laid out for the phone most people hold
items: The rows were measured on a Pixel, which is 411 points across; most phones are 360. Everything that had just been made to fit went back over the edge there - Mark watched onto a line of its own, the genre off the right of the tab row.

A pill on a narrow phone is smaller again: ten points of padding either side, four to the next one. Measured at 360 points: Resume 47:15, From start and Mark watched all stand on one row, ending well inside the screen.

title: The order and the genre fit across a phone
items: Pills on a phone are the same height with less width either side, so Home, Films, TV, the order and the genre all stand on one line at 1080 pixels instead of the genre hanging off the right. The television keeps the wider pills, which is the target a remote wants.

On a title's page Resume, From start and Mark watched stand on one row held upright, at any resume time: an hour and a half in the button says "Resume 1:37:04" and that was three points over the room, which put Mark watched on a line of its own. An episode's fourth button, Go to show, still takes the second line.

title: Search follows the tab it was typed on
items: In the browser, a search from the TV tab lists series and episodes before films, and one from Films lists films first. Somebody looking through TV who searches is looking for a programme, not for the film of the same name. From Home the server's own order stands, which puts first whatever the words asked for.
Reports hides itself while a library list is open, as it was meant to: the test named two tabs - "films" and "tv" - that the page does not have, so it never hid.

title: Search sits on the top row, and works from Home
items: The search box has moved up beside the name, where there is room for it, and it is on Home as well as Films and TV. From Home it looks through everything - films, series and episodes - rather than one section, since Home is not one.
The version number sits on a line above the name, which is the width the search box wanted; the P and the word keep the height and the spacing they had.

Typing dropped the fetch that the last letter started, and the screen said "the coroutine scope left the composition" instead of showing the results. A dropped fetch is not a failure and is passed on rather than reported.

title: The sort and the genre sit among the tabs
items: On Films and TV the order the list is in is fourth along and the genre fifth, straight after the TV tab, rather than at the end of a row that does not fit across a phone. They are the two controls somebody reaches for on the way into a list and the two that had to be scrolled to.
The search box stays at the end of the row.

title: Series with no date sort last in the app
items: Sorting television by Released or by Year put the unidentified series at the top. The server has always ordered its own share with those last; the app sorts the joined list again - several servers, one list - and that pass did not know about them. It does now, in both directions.

A series with no aired episode reported its date as the four letters "null", which the cards printed as "last aired null" and the sort read as a date. The server sends nothing instead, and the app reads a null as nothing.

title: 100% is a share of a 16:9 picture
items: Subtitle size is measured against a 16:9 picture as wide as the player rather than against the screen. A phone held upright is three times taller than the picture on it, so a share of the screen was text the height of a thumb; a browser window dragged tall and narrow had the same fault. On a television and a maximised window the two are the same number, so nothing moves there.
A scope film and a 16:9 film now draw the same size of text on the same screen.

Nothing is drawn until the shape of the picture is known. The black bar is worked out from the video's own width and height, and until the file has been read those are zero: the first cues were drawn in the wrong place and at the wrong size, and then jumped. Both clients hold them back instead - the browser until the metadata lands, the app until the first frame reports a size.

title: Subtitles draw with the phone upright
items: No cue was painted at all in portrait. Media3 draws into a child view of the subtitle view, and that child was left nought pixels tall - measured before the picture had a shape and never measured again. The view itself was the right size, the cues were there, and nothing was drawn. It is given the room the view has whenever the two disagree.

Cue heights are a share of the picture with the bottom of the box anchored at it, rather than a count of text rows. A row is still the step: one press of Position moves the text by one row of its own size, worked out from the size rather than counted by the player.
Reproduced and verified on a Pixel 6 emulator, upright and on its side, on a 16:9 file and a 2.4:1 one.

title: The subtitle language is the viewer's, not the browser's
items: The browser kept the language in its own storage and nowhere else, so a browser that had never been asked - a second machine, a cleared profile, a private window - started every title with subtitles off while the television had English. It now falls back to the language the server keeps for the viewer, which is the one the app already reads, and choosing here writes it there.
"Off" stays a choice of the browser that made it: the server keeps a language, not the absence of one.

Cue heights are worked out from the space the browser actually slides the box across, not from the height of the element. In a narrow window - a big black bar - the text sat a few pixels below the bottom edge of the picture.

title: A word while a track is being lifted out
items: A subtitle inside the film has to be extracted before it can be drawn, and on a large file that is minutes the first time. Both clients drew nothing and said nothing, which reads as broken subtitles - and rotating the phone, or anything else that happened to take that long, looked like the fix.

The player now says "Lifting the subtitles out of the film" after two and a half seconds, and stops as soon as the cues arrive. Every later playing of that track is served from the cache in about a tenth of a second.

title: Text size is measured from the picture, not the padding
items: Media3 measures a fractional text size against the view less its padding, and the padding carries the black bar. A phone held upright drew the first cues at 5% of the whole screen - several times the height of the picture - and they shrank as soon as the bar was padded out.
The fraction ignores the padding now and the picture is measured directly, so 100% is 5% of the height of the picture whatever shape the window is and whenever it settles.

title: Subtitles start at the right size in the app
items: The look is applied when the player view is built, not when the server answers. Until then the subtitle view used the file's own styling and Media3's default size and bottom padding, so the first cues were drawn too large and high and then jumped.
The look each title was drawn with is kept on the device and used as the starting point, so the first cue matches what the server is about to say.
A title never opened on this device starts at the general size for this kind of screen rather than the built-in default, which on a phone is a quarter smaller than most people watch with.

title: Heights are worked out again when the window changes
items: The browser now re-places the cues when the video element resizes, when full screen is entered or left, and when a stream of another shape arrives. The black bar under the picture is a number measured from the element, so a resized window was drawing subtitles with the old window's arithmetic.

In the app the same measurement is taken again on every layout of the subtitle view. It was taken once, when the picture size was first reported, and a layout listener left over from an earlier design then cleared it - so "bottom of the film" stopped counting from the film.

title: The subtitle look panel in the browser
items: No button in the Aa panel worked. The panel was built without the class the outside-press handler tests for, so every press inside it counted as a press outside: the panel closed and the click was swallowed. Both the class and the panel ids are tested now.
"Bottom of" - the film or the whole screen - is in the Aa panel, not only on the settings page.

A height or a base changed on the settings page with a film open now re-places the cues on screen. It used to take effect on the next film only, because those two settings live on the cues rather than in the stylesheet.
The panel's footer is one button: it resets this title's settings when there are any, and opens the defaults when there are not. The gear beside it is gone.

title: Subtitles are lifted out before they are wanted
items: Measured on a 7.6 GB film: 472 seconds to pull one text track out of the container the first time, 72 milliseconds every time after. That is where the waiting went - not in the listening, which is six seconds for the whole film, nor the correlating, which is under two.
The server now lifts every embedded text track out while nothing is playing and keeps it. It stops the moment somebody presses play, and picks up again when the machine is idle.
pd-warm-subs.py does the same on demand, for somebody who has just added a lot of films and would rather wait now than later.

App: Stop is in the subtitle menu while a measurement runs, not only over the picture; Reset appears whenever there is a correction to undo, even one made on another day. The verified tick moved to the right of the name.

Heights are measured from the picture by default, not the screen. On a film wider than the television the black bar under it is about 13% of the height and a line of text is 5%, so "Just up" was still inside the bar and looked like the very bottom - the setting and the screen disagreeing for a reason nobody could see. Where there is no bar nothing changes, and the Aa menu still offers either.
The film's page keeps to choosing a subtitle and saying which one: placing it and the auto tick are the player's, where the film is on screen to judge them against.

A subtitle inside the container is never measured by itself. It came with the release and is in step with it; measuring one costs minutes of reading the film to be told nought.
